parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the general solution of the differential equation d²y/dx² − 5 dy/dx + 6y = 0.
parts.working: M1 auxiliary equation m² − 5m + 6 = 0; A1 m = 2, 3 and y = Ae²ˣ + Be³ˣ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that y = 2 and dy/dx = 5 when x = 0, find the particular solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the general solution of d²y/dx² + 4 dy/dx + 13y = 0.
parts.working: M1 m² + 4m + 13 = 0; A1 m = −2 ± 3i; A1 y = e⁻²ˣ(A cos 3x + B sin 3x).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the particular solution for which y = 1 and dy/dx = 0 when x = 0.
parts.working: B1 A = 1; M1 differentiate: dy/dx at 0 = −2A + 3B = 0; A1 B = 2/3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the general solution of the differential equation d²y/dx² + 6 dy/dx + 9y = 18.
parts.working: M1 m² + 6m + 9 = 0, repeated root m = −3; A1 complementary function (A + Bx)e⁻³ˣ; M1 particular integral y = k gives 9k = 18; A1 y = (A + Bx)e⁻³ˣ + 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the limit of y as x → ∞.
parts.working: B1 (A + Bx)e⁻³ˣ → 0 so y → 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the complementary function for the differential equation d²y/dx² − dy/dx − 2y = 4x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find a particular integral of the form y = px + q, and hence write down the general solution.
parts.working: M1 substitute: −p − 2(px + q) = 4x; A1 p = −2, q = 1; A1 general solution y = Ae²ˣ + Be⁻ˣ − 2x + 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the particular solution of the differential equation d²y/dx² + 2 dy/dx + 5y = 10 cos x, given that y = 0 and dy/dx = 0 when x = 0.
parts.answer: y = e⁻ˣ(−2 cos 2x − (3/2) sin 2x) + 2 cos x + sin x
parts.working: M1 auxiliary equation m² + 2m + 5 = 0; A1 m = −1 ± 2i, CF e⁻ˣ(A cos 2x + B sin 2x); M1 PI p cos x + q sin x; M1 substitute and compare: 4p + 2q = 10, 4q − 2p = 0; A1 p = 2, q = 1; B1 general solution y = e⁻ˣ(A cos 2x + B sin 2x) + 2 cos x + sin x; M1 y(0) = 0: A + 2 = 0; A1 A = −2; M1 y′(0) = −A + 2B + 1 = 0; A1 B = −3/2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The displacement x metres of a model boat on a wave tank at time t seconds satisfies d²x/dt² + 4x = 8t². Find the general solution.
parts.working: M1 m² + 4 = 0, m = ±2i; A1 CF A cos 2t + B sin 2t; M1 PI at² + bt + c: 2a + 4(at² + bt + c) = 8t²; A1 a = 2, b = 0, c = −1; A1 general solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When t = 0, x = 0 and dx/dt = 2. Find x in terms of t.
parts.working: M1 A − 1 = 0 so A = 1; M1 dx/dt = −2A sin 2t + 2B cos 2t + 4t, so 2B = 2; A1 B = 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the particular solution of d²y/dx² − 3 dy/dx + 2y = 6e³ˣ for which y = 4 and dy/dx = 6 when x = 0.
parts.working: M1 m² − 3m + 2 = 0; A1 CF Aeˣ + Be²ˣ; M1 PI ke³ˣ: 9k − 9k + 2k = 6; A1 k = 3; M1 A + B + 3 = 4; M1 A + 2B + 9 = 6; A1 A = 5, B = −4; A1 final answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a particular integral of d²y/dx² + dy/dx − 6y = 10e²ˣ cannot be of the form ke²ˣ.
parts.answer: e²ˣ is part of the complementary function (m = 2 is a root of the auxiliary equation).
parts.working: B1 auxiliary equation m² + m − 6 = 0 has root 2, so ke²ˣ gives zero on the left side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using a particular integral of the form kxe²ˣ, find the general solution.
parts.working: B1 CF Ae²ˣ + Be⁻³ˣ; M1 y = kxe²ˣ, y′ = ke²ˣ(1 + 2x), y″ = ke²ˣ(4 + 4x); M1 substitute: ke²ˣ(4 + 4x + 1 + 2x − 6x) = 10e²ˣ; A1 5k = 10, k = 2; A1 general solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the solution of 4 d²y/dx² + 4 dy/dx + y = 3x + 2 for which y = 0 and dy/dx = 0 when x = 0.
parts.working: M1 4m² + 4m + 1 = 0; A1 m = −1/2 repeated, CF (A + Bx)e^(−x/2); M1 PI px + q: 4p + px + q = 3x + 2; A1 p = 3, q = −10; M1 y(0) = 0 gives A = 10; M1 differentiate and use y′(0) = 0: B − A/2 + 3 = 0; A1 B = 2; A1 final answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that, for large positive x, the graph of y approaches a straight line, and state its equation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that y = −x cos 3x is a particular integral of d²y/dx² + 9y = 6 sin 3x.
parts.working: M1 y′ = −cos 3x + 3x sin 3x; M1 y″ = 6 sin 3x + 9x cos 3x; A1 y″ + 9y = 6 sin 3x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the solution for which y = 0 and dy/dx = 1 when x = 0.
parts.working: B1 CF A cos 3x + B sin 3x; M1 y(0) = 0 gives A = 0; M1 y′(0) = 3B − 1 = 1; A1 B = 2/3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the behaviour of y as x becomes large.
parts.answer: y oscillates with amplitude that grows without bound (roughly proportional to x).
parts.working: B1 the term −x cos 3x dominates: oscillations of increasing amplitude.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The variable x satisfies d²x/dt² + 2 dx/dt + 2x = 4e⁻ᵗ, with x = 0 and dx/dt = 1 when t = 0. Find x in terms of t.
parts.answer: x = e⁻ᵗ(4 − 4 cos t + sin t)
parts.working: M1 m² + 2m + 2 = 0; A1 m = −1 ± i, CF e⁻ᵗ(A cos t + B sin t); M1 PI ke⁻ᵗ: k − 2k + 2k = 4; A1 k = 4; M1 x(0) = 0: A + 4 = 0; A1 A = −4; M1 differentiate, dx/dt at 0 = −A + B − 4 = 1; A1 B = 1; A1 final answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of x when t = π, and give it correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find a particular integral of d²y/dx² − 4 dy/dx + 4y = 8x² of the form ax² + bx + c.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that kx²e²ˣ is a particular integral of d²y/dx² − 4 dy/dx + 4y = e²ˣ for a suitable constant k, and find k.
parts.working: M1 y′ = ke²ˣ(2x + 2x²), y″ = ke²ˣ(2 + 8x + 4x²); M1 substitute: ke²ˣ(2 + 8x + 4x² − 8x − 8x² + 4x²) = 2ke²ˣ; A1 k = 1/2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence write down the general solution of d²y/dx² − 4 dy/dx + 4y = 8x² + e²ˣ.
parts.working: B1 CF (A + Bx)e²ˣ; B1 sum of both particular integrals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the solution of d²y/dx² − 2 dy/dx + 5y = 10 cos x for which y = 0 and dy/dx = 0 when x = 0. Hence find the exact value of y when x = π/2.
parts.working: M1 m² − 2m + 5 = 0; A1 m = 1 ± 2i, CF eˣ(A cos 2x + B sin 2x); M1 PI p cos x + q sin x; M1 compare: 4p − 2q = 10, 2p + 4q = 0; A1 p = 2, q = −1; M1 y(0) = 0: A + 2 = 0, A = −2; M1 y′(0) = A + 2B − 1 = 0; A1 B = 3/2; A1 solution; M1 substitute x = π/2: cos π = −1, sin π = 0; A1 2e^(π/2) − 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the solution of the differential equation dy/dx + 2y/x = 6x, for x > 0, given that y = 3 when x = 1. Give y in terms of x.
parts.working: M1 integrating factor e^(∫2/x dx) = x²; A1 d(x²y)/dx = 6x³; M1 integrate: x²y = 3x⁴/2 + c; A1 correct; M1 use (1, 3): c = 3/2; A1 y = 3x²/2 + 3/(2x²).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the general solution of dy/dx + 3y = 6e²ˣ.
parts.working: B1 integrating factor e³ˣ; M1 d(ye³ˣ)/dx = 6e⁵ˣ; M1 integrate: ye³ˣ = (6/5)e⁵ˣ + c; A1 y = (6/5)e²ˣ + ce⁻³ˣ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the particular solution for which y = 2 when x = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that an integrating factor for the differential equation dy/dx + y tan x = sec x, 0 ≤ x < π/2, is sec x.
parts.working: M1 e^(∫tan x dx) = e^(ln sec x); A1 = sec x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the solution for which y = 1 when x = 0.
parts.working: M1 d(y sec x)/dx = sec² x; A1 y sec x = tan x + c; M1 x = 0, y = 1 gives c = 1; A1 y = sin x + cos x.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the solution of x dy/dx + 3y = x² ln x, for x > 0, given that y = 0 when x = 1.
parts.working: M1 divide by x: dy/dx + 3y/x = x ln x; A1 integrating factor x³; M1 d(x³y)/dx = x⁴ ln x; M1 integrate by parts; A1 x³y = (x⁵/5) ln x − x⁵/25 + c; M1 use y(1) = 0; A1 c = 1/25; A1 final answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the solution of dy/dx + 2xy/(x² + 1) = 4x for which y = 3 when x = 0. Show that it can be written as y = x² + 1 + 2/(x² + 1).
parts.working: M1 integrating factor e^(ln(x² + 1)) = x² + 1; A1 d((x² + 1)y)/dx = 4x(x² + 1); M1 integrate: (x² + 1)y = x⁴ + 2x² + c; A1 correct; M1 y(0) = 3 gives c = 3; A1 y = (x⁴ + 2x² + 3)/(x² + 1); A1 = ((x² + 1)² + 2)/(x² + 1) = x² + 1 + 2/(x² + 1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: By writing u = x² + 1, find the least value of y, giving your answer in exact form.
parts.working: M1 y = u + 2/u with u ≥ 1; M1 dy/du = 1 − 2/u² = 0 gives u = √2 (≥ 1, so attainable); A1 least value √2 + 2/√2 = 2√2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the solution of dy/dx − 2y = e²ˣ cos x for which y = 1 when x = 0.
parts.working: B1 integrating factor e⁻²ˣ; M1 d(ye⁻²ˣ)/dx = cos x; A1 ye⁻²ˣ = sin x + c; M1 c = 1; A1 y = e²ˣ(sin x + 1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of y when x = π/2, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The variables x and y satisfy (x + 1) dy/dx + y = x(x + 1) for x ≥ 0, and y = 2 when x = 0. Find y in terms of x.
parts.working: M1 recognise the left side as d((x + 1)y)/dx (or divide and use integrating factor x + 1); A1 d((x + 1)y)/dx = x² + x; M1 integrate: (x + 1)y = x³/3 + x²/2 + c; A1 correct; M1 c = 2; A1 y = (2x³ + 3x² + 12)/(6(x + 1)).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of y when x = 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the solution of sin x dy/dx + 2y cos x = cos x, for 0 < x < π, given that y = 3 when x = π/6. Hence find the value of y when x = π/2.
parts.answer: y = 1/2 + (5/8) cosec² x; y = 9/8 when x = π/2
parts.working: M1 divide by sin x: dy/dx + 2y cot x = cot x; M1 integrating factor e^(2 ln sin x) = sin² x; A1 d(y sin² x)/dx = sin x cos x; M1 integrate: y sin² x = (1/2) sin² x + c; A1 correct; M1 use (π/6, 3): 3/4 = 1/8 + c, c = 5/8; A1 y = 1/2 + (5/8) cosec² x; A1 y(π/2) = 9/8.

practice.stem: A tank initially holds 100 litres of pure water. Salt solution with concentration 0.2 kg per litre flows in at 3 litres per minute, and the well-mixed solution flows out at 2 litres per minute. The tank does not overflow during the time considered. The mass of salt in the tank after t minutes is S kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that dS/dt + 2S/(100 + t) = 0.6.
parts.working: M1 inflow 3 × 0.2 = 0.6 kg/min; volume at time t is 100 + t litres, outflow 2 × S/(100 + t); A1 rearrange to given form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve the differential equation to find S in terms of t.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the mass of salt in the tank after 50 minutes, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the solution of x dy/dx − y = x³eˣ, for x > 0, given that y = 2 when x = 1.
parts.working: M1 divide by x: dy/dx − y/x = x²eˣ; A1 integrating factor 1/x; M1 d(y/x)/dx = xeˣ; M1 integrate by parts: y/x = (x − 1)eˣ + c; A1 correct; M1 use (1, 2): c = 2; A1 y = x(x − 1)eˣ + 2x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of y when x = 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that dy/dx > 0 for all x > 0.
parts.working: M1 dy/dx = (x² + x − 1)eˣ + 2; M1 for x ≥ 0.62 (where x² + x − 1 ≥ 0) every term is non-negative and 2 > 0; A1 for 0 < x < 0.62, x² + x − 1 > −1 and eˣ < 1.86, so (x² + x − 1)eˣ > −1.86 and dy/dx > 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the substitution y = vx to show that the differential equation dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(xy), x > 0, reduces to x dv/dx = 1/v.
parts.working: M1 dy/dx = v + x dv/dx; M1 right side = (1 + v²)/v = 1/v + v; A1 x dv/dx = 1/v.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find y² in terms of x, given that y = 2 when x = 1.
parts.working: M1 separate: v dv = dx/x; A1 v²/2 = ln x + c; M1 x = 1, v = 2: c = 2; A1 y² = 2x²(ln x + 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the substitution x = eᵗ transforms the differential equation x² d²y/dx² − 3x dy/dx + 3y = 6 into d²y/dt² − 4 dy/dt + 3y = 6.
parts.working: M1 dy/dx = e⁻ᵗ dy/dt, so x dy/dx = dy/dt; M1 d²y/dx² = e⁻²ᵗ(d²y/dt² − dy/dt); A1 x² d²y/dx² = d²y/dt² − dy/dt; A1 substitute: d²y/dt² − dy/dt − 3 dy/dt + 3y = 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the general solution for y in terms of x.
parts.working: M1 m² − 4m + 3 = 0, m = 1, 3; A1 CF Aeᵗ + Be³ᵗ; B1 PI y = 2; A1 y = Ax + Bx³ + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the substitution z = 1/y transforms dy/dx + y/x = xy² into dz/dx − z/x = −x.
parts.working: M1 dy/dx = −(1/z²) dz/dx; M1 substitute: −(1/z²) dz/dx + 1/(xz) = x/z²; A1 multiply by −z²: dz/dx − z/x = −x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find y in terms of x, given that y = 1/2 when x = 1.
parts.working: M1 integrating factor 1/x; A1 d(z/x)/dx = −1; M1 z/x = −x + c; M1 z = 2 at x = 1 gives c = 3; A1 y = 1/(3x − x²).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the substitution y = u/x transforms the differential equation x d²y/dx² + 2 dy/dx + 4xy = 0 into d²u/dx² + 4u = 0.
parts.working: M1 dy/dx = u′/x − u/x²; M1 d²y/dx² = u″/x − 2u′/x² + 2u/x³; M1 substitute: (u″ − 2u′/x + 2u/x²) + (2u′/x − 2u/x²) + 4u; A1 u″ + 4u = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find y in terms of x, given that y = 2/π when x = π/4 and y = 0 when x = π/2.
parts.working: M1 u = A cos 2x + B sin 2x; A1 y = (A cos 2x + B sin 2x)/x; M1 x = π/2: −A/(π/2) = 0, A = 0; M1 x = π/4: B/(π/4) = 2/π; A1 B = 1/2, y = sin 2x/(2x).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the substitution u = y² transforms the differential equation dy/dx − y = xe²ˣ/y into du/dx − 2u = 2xe²ˣ.
parts.working: M1 du/dx = 2y dy/dx; M1 multiply the equation by 2y: 2y dy/dx − 2y² = 2xe²ˣ; A1 du/dx − 2u = 2xe²ˣ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that y = 3 when x = 0 and y > 0, find y in terms of x.
parts.working: M1 integrating factor e⁻²ˣ; A1 d(ue⁻²ˣ)/dx = 2x; M1 ue⁻²ˣ = x² + c; M1 u = 9 at x = 0, c = 9; A1 y² = (x² + 9)e²ˣ so y = eˣ√(x² + 9).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The displacement x of a damped oscillator at time t satisfies d²x/dt² + 3 dx/dt + 2x = 4 sin 2t. Find the general solution.
parts.working: M1 m² + 3m + 2 = 0; A1 CF Ae⁻ᵗ + Be⁻²ᵗ; M1 PI p cos 2t + q sin 2t; M1 compare: −2p + 6q = 0, −6p − 2q = 4; A1 p = −3/5, q = −1/5; A1 general solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the motion for large values of t, and find the amplitude of this motion in exact form.
parts.answer: x ≈ −(3/5) cos 2t − (1/5) sin 2t: oscillation with period π and amplitude √10/5 ≈ 0.632
parts.working: M1 exponential terms → 0, so x approaches the particular integral; A1 oscillation of period π; A1 amplitude √((3/5)² + (1/5)²) = √10/5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the solution of d²y/dx² + 2 dy/dx + 10y = 20 + 18e⁻ˣ for which y = 0 and dy/dx = 0 when x = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to y as x → ∞, and explain why the answer does not depend on the initial conditions.
parts.working: B1 y → 2; B1 every other term contains the factor e⁻ˣ, which tends to 0 whatever the values of the arbitrary constants.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The region R is bounded by the curve y = 1/x, the x-axis and the lines x = 1 and x = 2. The interval [1, 2] is divided into 5 equal strips of width 0.2.
Using 5 rectangles each time, find an upper bound and a lower bound for the area of R. Give your answers correct to 4 decimal places.
parts.working:
B1: 1/x is decreasing, so the upper bound uses left ends (1, 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, 1.8) and the lower bound uses right ends (1.2, …, 2)
M1: 0.2(1 + 1/1.2 + 1/1.4 + 1/1.6 + 1/1.8)
A1: 0.7456
A1: lower 0.2(1/1.2 + … + 1/2) = 0.6456

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence write down an inequality satisfied by ln 2.
parts.working: B1: area of R = ∫₁² (1/x) dx = ln 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using 4 rectangles of width 1, find a lower bound and an upper bound for ∫₀⁴ √x dx. Give your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working:
M1: √x increasing: lower uses x = 0, 1, 2, 3; upper uses x = 1, 2, 3, 4
A1: lower = 0 + 1 + √2 + √3 = 4.15
A1: upper = 1 + √2 + √3 + 2 = 6.15

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of the integral and check that it lies between your bounds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that ∫₀¹ 1/(1 + x)³ dx = 3/8.
parts.working: B1: correct integration and limits

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using four rectangles of equal width, find a lower bound and an upper bound for this integral. Give your answers correct to 4 decimal places.
parts.working:
B1: 1/(1 + x)³ is decreasing on [0, 1], so the lower bound uses right ends x = 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1 and the upper bound uses left ends x = 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4
M1: (1/4)(64/125 + 8/27 + 64/343 + 1/8)
A1: lower 0.2800
A1: upper (1/4)(1 + 64/125 + 8/27 + 64/343) = 0.4987

parts.label: c
parts.text: Without further calculation of heights, show that the difference between your two bounds is exactly 7/32.
parts.working: B1: all other heights cancel, leaving (1/4)(1 − 1/8) = 7/32

parts.label: a
parts.text: The region under the curve y = 4 − x² from x = 0 to x = 2 is divided into 4 strips of width 0.5. Find the total area of the 4 upper rectangles and the total area of the 4 lower rectangles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact area of the region and the percentage error if the mean of the two bounds is used as an estimate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The integral I = ∫₀¹ e^(−x²) dx cannot be found exactly using elementary functions.
Explain why, for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, a set of rectangles using the values of e^(−x²) at the left-hand end of each strip gives an upper bound for I.
parts.answer: e^(−x²) is decreasing on [0, 1], so each left-end height is the largest value on its strip.
parts.working: B1: derivative −2x e^(−x²) ≤ 0, so the function is decreasing

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using 5 strips of equal width, find an upper bound and a lower bound for I, giving each correct to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to give an estimate of I, and state the greatest possible error in this estimate.
parts.working:
M1: mean of bounds (0.808 + 0.681)/2
A1: 0.744 ± 0.063 (half the gap; exact gap is 0.2(1 − e⁻¹))

parts.label: a
parts.text:
By considering the area under the curve y = 1/x, with rectangles of width 1, show that
ln(n + 1) < 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … + 1/n < 1 + ln n, for n ≥ 2.
parts.working:
M1: rectangles of width 1 with heights 1/r on [r, r + 1] lie above the curve (1/x decreasing)
A1: Σ_{r=1}^{n} 1/r > ∫₁^(n+1) dx/x = ln(n + 1)
M1: rectangles with heights 1/r on [r − 1, r] for r = 2, …, n lie below the curve
A1: Σ_{r=2}^{n} 1/r < ∫₁ⁿ dx/x = ln n
A1: add 1 to complete the result

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find, correct to 2 decimal places, a lower bound and an upper bound for 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … + 1/1000.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
By considering rectangles of width 1 and the curve y = √x, show that
(2/3)n^(3/2) < √1 + √2 + √3 + … + √n < (2/3)[(n + 1)^(3/2) − 1].
parts.working:
M1: √x increasing, so rectangle on [r − 1, r] with height √r lies above the curve: Σ√r > ∫₀ⁿ √x dx
A1: = (2/3)n^(3/2)
M1: rectangle on [r, r + 1] with height √r lies below the curve: Σ√r < ∫₁^(n+1) √x dx
A1: = (2/3)[(n + 1)^(3/2) − 1]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find bounds for √1 + √2 + … + √400, giving each to the nearest whole number in a way that keeps the inequality true.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Let Sₙ = 1/(n + 1) + 1/(n + 2) + … + 1/(2n). Use rectangles under or above the graph of y = 1/x to show that
ln((2n + 1)/(n + 1)) < Sₙ < ln 2.
parts.working:
M1: rectangles of width 1, height 1/r on [r − 1, r], r = n + 1, …, 2n, lie under the curve: Sₙ < ∫ₙ^(2n) dx/x
A1: = ln 2
M1: height 1/r on [r, r + 1] lies above the curve: Sₙ > ∫_(n+1)^(2n+1) dx/x
A1: = ln((2n + 1)/(n + 1))

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the lower bound for S₅₀ given by this result, correct to 4 decimal places, and deduce the limit of Sₙ as n → ∞.
parts.working:
B1: ln(101/51) = 0.6833
B1: (2n + 1)/(n + 1) → 2, so both bounds → ln 2; limit ln 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that ∫₁ⁿ ln x dx = n ln n − n + 1.
parts.working:
M1: integrate by parts: [x ln x]₁ⁿ − ∫₁ⁿ 1 dx
A1: n ln n − (n − 1) = n ln n − n + 1 (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
By considering rectangles of width 1, show that
n ln n − n + 1 < ln(n!) < (n + 1) ln(n + 1) − n.
parts.working:
M1: ln x increasing; heights ln r on [r − 1, r] lie above the curve: ln 2 + … + ln n > ∫₁ⁿ ln x dx
A1: ln(n!) > n ln n − n + 1
M1: heights ln r on [r, r + 1] lie below the curve: ln 1 + … + ln n < ∫₁^(n+1) ln x dx
A1: = (n + 1) ln(n + 1) − (n + 1) + 1 = (n + 1)ln(n + 1) − n

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence find bounds for 10!, giving each correct to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Use rectangles of width 1 under or above the curve y = 1/√x to show that
2√(n + 1) − 2 < Σ_{r=1}^{n} 1/√r < 2√n − 1.
parts.working:
M1: 1/√x decreasing; rectangles of height 1/√r on [r, r + 1] lie above the curve: Σ > ∫₁^(n+1) x^(−1/2) dx
A1: = 2√(n + 1) − 2
M1: for r ≥ 2 rectangles on [r − 1, r] lie below: Σ_{r=2}^{n} < ∫₁ⁿ x^(−1/2) dx = 2√n − 2
A1: add the first term 1: Σ < 2√n − 1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence show that 18.0 < Σ_{r=1}^{100} 1/√r < 19.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The interval [0, 1] is divided into n equal strips. Show that the upper rectangle sum Uₙ for the area under y = x² from x = 0 to x = 1 is
Uₙ = (n + 1)(2n + 1)/(6n²).
parts.working:
M1: Uₙ = (1/n) Σ_{r=1}^{n} (r/n)² (right ends, since x² is increasing)
M1: = (1/n³) × n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6
A1: = (n + 1)(2n + 1)/(6n²) (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find a similar expression for the lower sum Lₙ, and show that Uₙ − Lₙ = 1/n.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the least value of n for which the difference between the bounds is less than 0.01, and state the limit of Uₙ as n → ∞.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The region under y = eˣ from x = 0 to x = 1 is divided into n strips of equal width. Show that the sum of the areas of the lower rectangles is
Lₙ = (e − 1) / [n(e^(1/n) − 1)].
parts.working:
M1: eˣ increasing: Lₙ = (1/n)[1 + e^(1/n) + e^(2/n) + … + e^((n−1)/n)]
M1: geometric series with ratio e^(1/n), n terms
A1: sum = (e − 1)/(e^(1/n) − 1)
A1: Lₙ = (e − 1)/[n(e^(1/n) − 1)] (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find L₁₀ correct to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: By writing h = 1/n, find the limit of Lₙ as n → ∞, and explain why this is the value you should expect.
parts.working:
M1: Lₙ = (e − 1) × h/(eʰ − 1)
M1: h/(eʰ − 1) → 1 as h → 0 (eʰ − 1 ≈ h, or l'Hôpital / series)
A1: limit e − 1, which is the exact area ∫₀¹ eˣ dx

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The area A under the curve y = 1/x² between x = 1 and x = 2 is estimated using N rectangles of equal width, giving an upper bound U and a lower bound L.
Show that U − L = 3/(4N).
parts.working:
M1: decreasing function; U uses left ends x = 1, 1 + h, …, 2 − h and L uses right ends 1 + h, …, 2, with h = 1/N
M1: all terms cancel except h[f(1) − f(2)]
A1: (1/N)(1 − 1/4) = 3/(4N) (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the least value of N for which U − L < 0.01.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the exact value of A and verify that U − A < 3/(4N) for N = 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let Sₙ = Σ_{r=1}^{n} n/(n² + r²). Show that Sₙ is the total area of n rectangles of width 1/n under the curve y = 1/(1 + x²) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, and explain why Sₙ < π/4.
parts.answer: Sₙ = (1/n)Σ 1/(1 + (r/n)²), a right-end (lower) rectangle sum for a decreasing function, so Sₙ < ∫₀¹ dx/(1 + x²) = π/4.
parts.working:
M1: n/(n² + r²) = (1/n) × 1/(1 + (r/n)²)
A1: heights at x = r/n, width 1/n
B1: 1/(1 + x²) is decreasing on [0, 1], so right ends give rectangles below the curve
B1: ∫₀¹ dx/(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹1 = π/4

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the corresponding upper sum Tₙ in terms of n, and hence use n = 4 to show that 2.88 < π < 3.39.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the limit of Sₙ as n → ∞.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let Iₙ = ∫₁ᵉ x(ln x)ⁿ dx for n ≥ 0. Show that 2Iₙ = e² − nIₙ₋₁ for n ≥ 1.
parts.working:
M1: by parts with u = (ln x)ⁿ, dv = x dx
A1: Iₙ = [(x²/2)(ln x)ⁿ]₁ᵉ − ∫₁ᵉ (x²/2) · n(ln x)ⁿ⁻¹ (1/x) dx
A1: = e²/2 − (n/2)Iₙ₋₁, so 2Iₙ = e² − nIₙ₋₁ (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of I₃.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let Iₙ = ∫₀¹ xⁿ eˣ dx for n ≥ 0. Show that Iₙ = e − nIₙ₋₁ for n ≥ 1.
parts.working:
M1: by parts with u = xⁿ, dv = eˣ dx
A1: [xⁿeˣ]₀¹ − n∫₀¹ xⁿ⁻¹eˣ dx
A1: = e − nIₙ₋₁ (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find I₄ in the form ae + b, where a and b are integers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let Iₙ = ∫₀^(π/2) sinⁿx dx. By writing sinⁿx = sinⁿ⁻¹x sin x, show that nIₙ = (n − 1)Iₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 2.
parts.working:
M1: by parts: u = sinⁿ⁻¹x, dv = sin x dx
A1: [−sinⁿ⁻¹x cos x]₀^(π/2) + (n − 1)∫ sinⁿ⁻²x cos²x dx
M1: cos²x = 1 − sin²x
A1: Iₙ = (n − 1)(Iₙ₋₂ − Iₙ) ⇒ nIₙ = (n − 1)Iₙ₋₂ (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of I₆.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of ∫₀^(π/2) sin⁴x cos²x dx.
parts.working:
M1: sin⁴x cos²x = sin⁴x − sin⁶x, so integral = I₄ − I₆
A1: 3π/16 − 5π/32 = π/32

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let Iₙ = ∫₀^(π/2) xⁿ cos x dx for n ≥ 0. Show that Iₙ = (π/2)ⁿ − n(n − 1)Iₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 2.
parts.working:
M1: by parts: [xⁿ sin x]₀^(π/2) − n∫ xⁿ⁻¹ sin x dx = (π/2)ⁿ − n∫ xⁿ⁻¹ sin x dx
M1: by parts again: ∫ xⁿ⁻¹ sin x dx = [−xⁿ⁻¹cos x] + (n − 1)∫ xⁿ⁻² cos x dx
A1: boundary terms vanish (cos(π/2) = 0, and x^(n−1) = 0 at 0)
A1: Iₙ = (π/2)ⁿ − n(n − 1)Iₙ₋₂ (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of I₄, and give it correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let Iₙ = ∫₀¹ (1 − x²)ⁿ dx for n ≥ 0. Show that (2n + 1)Iₙ = 2nIₙ₋₁ for n ≥ 1.
parts.working:
M1: by parts with u = (1 − x²)ⁿ, dv = dx: Iₙ = [x(1 − x²)ⁿ]₀¹ + 2n∫₀¹ x²(1 − x²)ⁿ⁻¹ dx
A1: boundary term 0
M1: x² = 1 − (1 − x²)
A1: Iₙ = 2n(Iₙ₋₁ − Iₙ)
A1: (2n + 1)Iₙ = 2nIₙ₋₁ (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find I₅ as a fraction in its lowest terms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the substitution x = sin θ, deduce the exact value of ∫₀^(π/2) cos¹¹θ dθ.
parts.working:
M1: dx = cos θ dθ, (1 − x²)⁵ = cos¹⁰θ, so I₅ = ∫₀^(π/2) cos¹¹θ dθ
A1: 256/693

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let Iₙ = ∫₀^(π/4) tanⁿx dx. Show that Iₙ + Iₙ₋₂ = 1/(n − 1) for n ≥ 2.
parts.working:
M1: Iₙ + Iₙ₋₂ = ∫ tanⁿ⁻²x (tan²x + 1) dx = ∫ tanⁿ⁻²x sec²x dx
M1: = [tanⁿ⁻¹x/(n − 1)]₀^(π/4)
A1: = 1/(n − 1) (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of I₅.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Iₙ > Iₙ₊₁ for every n ≥ 0, and hence show that 1/(2(n + 1)) < Iₙ < 1/(2(n − 1)) for n ≥ 2.
parts.answer: 0 ≤ tan x ≤ 1 on [0, π/4] so tanⁿ⁺¹x ≤ tanⁿx; then 2Iₙ < Iₙ + Iₙ₋₂ = 1/(n − 1) and 2Iₙ > Iₙ + Iₙ₊₂ = 1/(n + 1).
parts.working:
B1: 0 < tan x < 1 for 0 < x < π/4, so Iₙ₊₁ < Iₙ
M1: Iₙ₊₂ < Iₙ < Iₙ₋₂ used with the reduction formula
A1: 1/(n + 1) < 2Iₙ < 1/(n − 1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the exact value of ∫₀³ 1/√(x² + 9) dx, giving your answer as a natural logarithm.
parts.working:
M1: standard integral sinh⁻¹(x/3)
A1: sinh⁻¹1 − 0
A1: ln(1 + √2)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of ∫₀³ 1/(x² + 9) dx.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By completing the square, find the exact value of ∫₃⁵ 1/√(x² − 2x − 3) dx, giving your answer in logarithmic form.
parts.working:
B1: x² − 2x − 3 = (x − 1)² − 4
M1: ∫ dx/√((x − 1)² − 2²) = cosh⁻¹((x − 1)/2)
A1: cosh⁻¹2 − cosh⁻¹1 = cosh⁻¹2
A1: ln(2 + √3)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The integrand is not defined at x = 3. Explain why the integral nevertheless has a finite value.
parts.answer: The integrand is undefined at x = 3 (denominator 0), but cosh⁻¹((x − 1)/2) → 0 as x → 3⁺, so the limit exists.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the substitution x = 2 sin θ to show that ∫₀¹ x²/√(4 − x²) dx = π/3 − √3/2.
parts.working:
B1: dx = 2cos θ dθ; limits θ = 0 to π/6
M1: integrand becomes 4sin²θ × 2cos θ/(2cos θ) = 4sin²θ
M1: 4sin²θ = 2 − 2cos 2θ
A1: [2θ − sin 2θ]₀^(π/6)
A1: π/3 − √3/2 (AG)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the substitution u = eˣ to find the exact value of ∫₀^(ln 2) 1/(eˣ + 4e⁻ˣ) dx.
parts.working:
M1: multiply top and bottom by eˣ: eˣ/(e²ˣ + 4)
M1: u = eˣ, du = eˣ dx, limits 1 to 2: ∫₁² du/(u² + 4)
A1: [(1/2)tan⁻¹(u/2)]₁²
A1: (1/2)(π/4 − tan⁻¹(1/2))
A1: (or (1/2)tan⁻¹(1/3), using the tan subtraction formula)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give your answer correct to 4 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the exact length of the arc of the curve y = cosh x from x = 0 to x = ln 3.
parts.working:
M1: s = ∫√(1 + sinh²x) dx = ∫ cosh x dx
A1: [sinh x]₀^(ln 3)
M1: sinh(ln 3) = (3 − 1/3)/2
A1: 4/3

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = x²/2 − (1/4) ln x for x > 0. Show that 1 + (dy/dx)² = (x + 1/(4x))².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact length of the arc of C from x = 1 to x = 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A curve is defined parametrically by x = t², y = (2/3)t³, for 0 ≤ t ≤ √3. Show that (dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)² = 4t²(1 + t²).
parts.working:
M1: dx/dt = 2t, dy/dt = 2t²
A1: 4t² + 4t⁴ = 4t²(1 + t²) (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact length of the curve.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A wire is bent into the shape of this curve, with lengths in centimetres. A second wire of the same shape is made from the curve for 0 ≤ t ≤ T. Find T if the second wire is exactly half as long as the first.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The arc of the curve y = 2√x from x = 0 to x = 3 is rotated through 2π radians about the x-axis. Find the exact area of the surface generated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A lampshade is modelled by rotating the arc of y = cosh x between x = 0 and x = 1 through 2π radians about the x-axis (units are decimetres). Show that the curved surface area is π(1 + (1/2)sinh 2).
parts.working:
M1: √(1 + sinh²x) = cosh x
M1: S = 2π∫₀¹ cosh²x dx
M1: cosh²x = (1 + cosh 2x)/2
A1: π[x + (1/2)sinh 2x]₀¹
A1: π(1 + (1/2)sinh 2) (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find this area correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A curve is given parametrically by x = cos³t, y = sin³t, for 0 ≤ t ≤ π/2. Show that (dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)² = 9sin²t cos²t.
parts.working:
M1: dx/dt = −3cos²t sin t, dy/dt = 3sin²t cos t
M1: 9cos⁴t sin²t + 9sin⁴t cos²t = 9sin²t cos²t(cos²t + sin²t)
A1: 9sin²t cos²t (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The curve is rotated through 2π radians about the x-axis. Find the exact area of the surface generated.
parts.working:
M1: S = 2π∫ y √(…) dt = 2π∫₀^(π/2) sin³t × 3 sin t cos t dt
A1: 6π∫₀^(π/2) sin⁴t cos t dt
M1: [sin⁵t/5]₀^(π/2)
A1: 6π/5

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (x² + 3)/(x − 1). Find the coordinates of the stationary points of C.
parts.working: M1 quotient rule: dy/dx = (2x(x − 1) − (x² + 3))/(x − 1)²; A1 = (x² − 2x − 3)/(x − 1)²; M1 set numerator = 0: (x − 3)(x + 1) = 0; A1 (−1, −2) and (3, 6).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the nature of each stationary point and hence state the set of values that y cannot take.
parts.answer: (−1, −2) is a maximum, (3, 6) is a minimum; y cannot take values with −2 < y < 6
parts.working: M1 sign of dy/dx either side (or second derivative); A1 max at (−1, −2), min at (3, 6); B1 −2 < y < 6 excluded (the two branches lie either side of x = 1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (x − 2)/(x² + 5). By considering a quadratic equation in x, show that −1/2 ≤ y ≤ 1/10 for all real x.
parts.working: M1 rearrange: yx² − x + (5y + 2) = 0; M1 real x requires discriminant ≥ 0: 1 − 4y(5y + 2) ≥ 0; A1 20y² + 8y − 1 ≤ 0, i.e. (10y − 1)(2y + 1) ≤ 0; A1 −1/2 ≤ y ≤ 1/10.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the coordinates of the turning points of C.
parts.working: M1 at the extreme values the quadratic has a repeated root x = 1/(2y); A1 y = 1/10 gives x = 5, y = −1/2 gives x = −1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (x² + x + 1)/(x² − x + 1). Explain why C has no vertical asymptotes and state the equation of its horizontal asymptote.
parts.answer: x² − x + 1 = (x − 1/2)² + 3/4 > 0, so the denominator is never zero; horizontal asymptote y = 1
parts.working: B1 completing the square (or discriminant −3 < 0); B1 y = 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that 1/3 ≤ y ≤ 3 for all real x.
parts.working: M1 (y − 1)x² − (y + 1)x + (y − 1) = 0; M1 discriminant (y + 1)² − 4(y − 1)² ≥ 0; A1 (3 − y)(3y − 1) ≥ 0; A1 1/3 ≤ y ≤ 3 (y = 1 also gives real x = 0).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of C.
parts.working: M1 repeated root x = (y + 1)/(2(y − 1)); A1 (1, 3) and (−1, 1/3).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (x² + k)/(x − 2), where k is a constant and k ≠ −4. Find the set of values of k for which C has no stationary points.
parts.working: M1 dy/dx = (x² − 4x − k)/(x − 2)²; M1 no stationary points when discriminant 16 + 4k < 0; A1 k < −4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In the case k = 5, find the coordinates of the stationary points of C and the set of values of y for which no point of C exists.
parts.answer: (−1, −2) maximum, (5, 10) minimum; no point of C for −2 < y < 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: The function f is defined for all real x by f(x) = (x² − 3x)/(x² + 3). Find the range of f.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the x-coordinate at which f takes its greatest value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (ax + 1)/(x² + 1), where a is a positive constant. Show that the set of values taken by y is (1 − √(1 + a²))/2 ≤ y ≤ (1 + √(1 + a²))/2.
parts.working: M1 yx² − ax + (y − 1) = 0; M1 discriminant a² − 4y(y − 1) ≥ 0; A1 4y² − 4y − a² ≤ 0; A1 roots y = (1 ± √(1 + a²))/2, so y lies between them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that the greatest value of y is 3, find the exact value of a and the least value of y.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the exact x-coordinates of the stationary points of C for this value of a.
parts.working: M1 repeated root x = a/(2y); A1 y = 3 gives x = 2√6/6 = √6/3, y = −2 gives x = −2√6/4 = −√6/2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (x² − 2x + λ)/(x − 3), where λ is a constant and λ ≠ −3. Show that C has two stationary points if and only if λ > −3.
parts.working: M1 dy/dx = ((2x − 2)(x − 3) − (x² − 2x + λ))/(x − 3)²; A1 numerator x² − 6x + 6 − λ; M1 two distinct roots iff 36 − 4(6 − λ) > 0; A1 12 + 4λ > 0 so λ > −3 (and x = 3 is not a root since λ ≠ −3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: For λ = 1, find the coordinates of the stationary points and state the set of values of y for which the line y = k does not meet C.
parts.working: M1 x² − 6x + 5 = 0; A1 x = 1, 5; A1 (1, 0) and (5, 8); B1 the line misses C for 0 < k < 8.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why, for λ = 1, the curve touches the x-axis.
parts.answer: The numerator is (x − 1)², so y = 0 only at x = 1, which is a stationary point
parts.working: B1 repeated root of the numerator at the maximum point (1, 0).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the inequality (x + 3)/(x − 1) < 2.
parts.working: M1 bring to one side: (x + 3)/(x − 1) − 2 < 0; A1 (5 − x)/(x − 1) < 0; M1 critical values 1 and 5 with sign analysis; A1 x < 1 or x > 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the inequality 2/(x + 1) ≤ 1/(x − 3).
parts.working: M1 combine: (2(x − 3) − (x + 1))/((x + 1)(x − 3)) ≤ 0; A1 (x − 7)/((x + 1)(x − 3)) ≤ 0; M1 critical values −1, 3, 7; M1 sign table; A1 x < −1 or 3 < x ≤ 7 (x = 7 included, −1 and 3 excluded).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the exact set of values of x satisfying (x² + 2)/(x + 1) > 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the inequality |(2x − 1)/(x + 2)| < 1.
parts.working: M1 −1 < (2x − 1)/(x + 2) < 1; M1 (x − 3)/(x + 2) < 0 gives −2 < x < 3; M1 (3x + 1)/(x + 2) > 0 gives x < −2 or x > −1/3; A1 critical values correct; A1 intersection −1/3 < x < 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the inequality x/(x − 2) ≤ x/(x + 1).
parts.working: M1 x/(x − 2) − x/(x + 1) ≤ 0; A1 3x/((x − 2)(x + 1)) ≤ 0; M1 critical values −1, 0, 2 (do not cancel x); M1 sign table; A1 x < −1 or 0 ≤ x < 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the exact set of values of x for which |(x² − 4)/(x − 1)| > 3.
parts.working: M1 split into (x² − 4)/(x − 1) > 3 or (x² − 4)/(x − 1) < −3; M1 (x² − 3x − 1)/(x − 1) > 0; A1 (3 − √13)/2 < x < 1 or x > (3 + √13)/2; M1 (x² + 3x − 7)/(x − 1) < 0; A1 x < (−3 − √37)/2 or 1 < x < (−3 + √37)/2; M1 combine the two sets; A1 all four intervals correct (x = 1 excluded).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that a is a positive constant, solve the inequality (x + a)/(x − a) > (x − a)/(x + a), giving your answer in terms of a.
parts.working: M1 combine over (x − a)(x + a); A1 numerator (x + a)² − (x − a)² = 4ax; M1 4ax/((x − a)(x + a)) > 0 with critical values −a, 0, a; M1 sign analysis using a > 0; A1 −a < x < 0 or x > a.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (x − 2)/(x + 1). State the equations of the asymptotes of C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the gradient of C is positive at every point.
parts.working: M1 quotient rule: ((x + 1) − (x − 2))/(x + 1)²; A1 3/(x + 1)², positive for all x ≠ −1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sketch C, stating the coordinates of the points where it meets the axes.
parts.answer: Two branches in the top-left and bottom-right regions formed by the asymptotes; crosses axes at (2, 0) and (0, −2)
parts.working: B1 both branches correct shape approaching asymptotes; B1 (2, 0); B1 (0, −2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (x² + 1)/(x² − 4). State the equations of the three asymptotes of C.
parts.working: B1 both vertical asymptotes; B1 y = 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find dy/dx and hence find the coordinates of the stationary point of C, stating its nature.
parts.working: M1 quotient rule; A1 −10x/(x² − 4)²; A1 (0, −1/4) maximum (gradient changes from + to −).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sketch C.
parts.answer: Symmetrical about the y-axis; central branch below the x-axis between x = −2 and x = 2 with maximum (0, −1/4); outer branches above y = 1, approaching y = 1 from above as x → ±∞; no x-intercepts
parts.working: B1 central branch; B1 outer branches; B1 symmetry and no x-intercepts, (0, −1/4) labelled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (x² − x − 2)/(x − 3). Express y in the form ax + b + c/(x − 3) and hence state the equations of the asymptotes of C.
parts.answer: y = x + 2 + 4/(x − 3); asymptotes x = 3 and y = x + 2
parts.working: M1 division; A1 x + 2 + 4/(x − 3); A1 both asymptotes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sketch C, stating the coordinates of any points where C meets the axes.
parts.answer: Left branch: rises from −∞, crosses (−1, 0), maximum (1, 1), crosses (2, 0), falls to −∞ as x → 3⁻; it passes through (0, 2/3). Right branch: minimum (5, 9), approaching x = 3 and y = x + 2
parts.working: B1 left branch shape with maximum; B1 right branch with minimum; B1 intercepts (−1, 0), (2, 0), (0, 2/3).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = 3x/(x² + x + 1). Show that −3 ≤ y ≤ 1.
parts.working: M1 yx² + (y − 3)x + y = 0; M1 (y − 3)² − 4y² ≥ 0; A1 (y + 3)(y − 1) ≤ 0 (after rearranging −3y² − 6y + 9 ≥ 0); A1 −3 ≤ y ≤ 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the turning points of C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sketch C, stating the equation of its asymptote.
parts.answer: Passes through the origin; minimum (−1, −3), maximum (1, 1); y → 0 as x → ±∞ (asymptote y = 0), approaching from below on the left and from above on the right
parts.working: B1 shape through O with both turning points; B1 asymptote y = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (x² + 2x − 3)/(x² − 2x − 3). Find the equations of the asymptotes of C and the coordinates of the points where C meets the axes.
parts.answer: Asymptotes x = 3, x = −1, y = 1; meets axes at (−3, 0), (1, 0) and (0, 1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that dy/dx = −4(x² + 3)/((x − 3)²(x + 1)²) and deduce that C has no stationary points.
parts.working: M1 quotient rule; A1 simplified result; A1 x² + 3 > 0 so dy/dx < 0 for all x in the domain.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find where C crosses its horizontal asymptote, and sketch C.
parts.answer: Crosses y = 1 at (0, 1). Left branch (x < −1): decreasing from y = 1⁻ through (−3, 0) to −∞; middle branch: decreasing from +∞ through (0, 1) and (1, 0) to −∞; right branch (x > 3): decreasing from +∞ towards y = 1
parts.working: B1 x² + 2x − 3 = x² − 2x − 3 gives x = 0; B1 three decreasing branches; B1 correct approach to all asymptotes with intercepts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (x² − 3x + k)/(x − 1), where k is a constant. Given that C has a stationary point where x = 3, find k.
parts.working: M1 dy/dx numerator (2x − 3)(x − 1) − (x² − 3x + k) = x² − 2x + 3 − k; M1 substitute x = 3; A1 k = 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For this value of k, find the coordinates of both stationary points and the equations of the asymptotes.
parts.answer: (3, 3) and (−1, −5); asymptotes x = 1 and y = x − 2

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that C does not meet the x-axis, and sketch C.
parts.answer: Discriminant of x² − 3x + 6 is 9 − 24 < 0. Left branch has maximum (−1, −5) and passes through (0, −6); right branch has minimum (3, 3)
parts.working: B1 discriminant −15 < 0; B1 left branch with max and y-intercept −6; B1 right branch with min, asymptotes shown.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the equations of the asymptotes of the curve y = (3x + 2)/(x − 4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the point where the curve meets the y-axis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (2x² + 3x − 1)/(x + 2). Find the equations of the asymptotes of C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State, with a reason, whether the curve lies above or below its oblique asymptote for large positive x.
parts.answer: Above, because y − (2x − 1) = 1/(x + 2) > 0 for large positive x
parts.working: B1 correct conclusion with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (x³ + 1)/(x² − 4). Find the equations of all the asymptotes of C.
parts.working: B1 x = ±2; M1 x³ + 1 = x(x² − 4) + 4x + 1; A1 y = x + (4x + 1)/(x² − 4); A1 oblique asymptote y = x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the point where C crosses its oblique asymptote.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve y = (ax² + bx + 3)/(x − 1) has oblique asymptote y = 2x + 5. Find the values of the constants a and b.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the equation of the other asymptote and determine, with reasons, whether the curve has any stationary points.
parts.answer: x = 1; yes: dy/dx = 2 − 8/(x − 1)² = 0 gives x = 3 or x = −1, so two stationary points
parts.working: B1 x = 1; M1 y = 2x + 5 + 8/(x − 1) differentiated; A1 (x − 1)² = 4 has two real solutions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (λx² + 5x − 2)/(x² − x − 6), where λ is a constant. Find the values of λ for which C has only one vertical asymptote.
parts.working: M1 numerator must vanish at x = 3 or x = −2; A1 x = −2: 4λ − 12 = 0, λ = 3; A1 x = 3: 9λ + 13 = 0, λ = −13/9.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the equation of the horizontal asymptote of C in terms of λ.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Given that C crosses its horizontal asymptote at x = 2, find λ and verify the crossing point.
parts.working: M1 λx² + 5x − 2 = λ(x² − x − 6) gives x(λ + 5) = 2 − 6λ; M1 substitute x = 2; A1 λ = −1, and y(2) = 4/(−4) = −1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (kx² + 3x − 1)/(x + k), where k is a positive constant. Show that the oblique asymptote of C is y = kx + 3 − k².
parts.working: M1 divide by x + k; A1 quotient kx + (3 − k²); A1 remainder k³ − 3k − 1 (non-zero for the values used), so asymptote y = kx + 3 − k².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that the oblique asymptote passes through the point (1, 3), find k.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For this value of k, show that C has no stationary points.
parts.working: M1 rewrite with remainder −3; M1 differentiate; A1 dy/dx > 0 for all x ≠ −1, so no stationary points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sketch the curve y = |(x − 2)/(x + 1)|, stating the equations of its asymptotes and the coordinates of the points where it meets the axes.
parts.answer: Asymptotes x = −1 and y = 1; touches the x-axis at (2, 0); meets the y-axis at (0, 2). The part of y = (x − 2)/(x + 1) between x = −1 and x = 2 is reflected in the x-axis
parts.working: B1 correct asymptotes; B1 reflected section above axis with cusp at (2, 0); B1 (0, 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve the equation |(x − 2)/(x + 1)| = 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence solve the inequality |(x − 2)/(x + 1)| < 2.
parts.working: M1 use the sketch; A1 x < −4 or x > 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = f(x), where f(x) = (x² + 3)/(x − 1). The stationary points of C are (−1, −2) and (3, 6). Sketch the curve y = 1/f(x), stating the coordinates of its stationary points and any points where it meets the axes.
parts.answer: y = (x − 1)/(x² + 3): no vertical asymptotes, asymptote y = 0; passes through (1, 0) and (0, −1/3); minimum (−1, −1/2) and maximum (3, 1/6)
parts.working: B1 y = 0 asymptote and no vertical asymptotes (x² + 3 > 0); B1 (1, 0) and (0, −1/3); B1 (−1, −1/2) minimum; B1 (3, 1/6) maximum; B1 correct overall shape.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the set of values of k for which the equation 1/f(x) = k has two distinct real roots.
parts.working: M1 use extreme values of 1/f; A1 −1/2 < k < 1/6 with k ≠ 0 (k = 0 gives only x = 1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The function f is defined by f(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 2). Sketch the curve y = f(|x|), stating the equations of its asymptotes and the coordinates of any intersections with the axes.
parts.answer: Symmetrical about the y-axis; asymptotes x = 2, x = −2 and y = 1; meets the y-axis at (0, −1/2); does not meet the x-axis
parts.working: B1 right half from y = f(x) for x ≥ 0; B1 reflection in the y-axis; B1 asymptotes; B1 (0, −1/2) and no x-intercepts (x = −1 is not in the range |x| ≥ 0).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve the inequality f(|x|) > 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = (x² − x − 2)/(x − 3). It has asymptotes x = 3 and y = x + 2, a maximum point (1, 1) and a minimum point (5, 9), and it crosses the x-axis at (−1, 0) and (2, 0). Sketch the curve y = |(x² − x − 2)/(x − 3)|.
parts.answer: For x < 3: the branch is reflected wherever it is below the x-axis, giving cusps at (−1, 0) and (2, 0), a local maximum (1, 1), and y → +∞ as x → 3⁻ and as x → −∞ (approaching y = −x − 2). For x > 3 the branch is unchanged with minimum (5, 9)
parts.working: B1 reflection of the parts below the axis; B1 asymptotes x = 3, y = x + 2 and y = −x − 2; B1 key points labelled.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the set of values of k for which the equation |(x² − x − 2)/(x − 3)| = k has exactly four distinct real roots.
parts.working: M1 count intersections of y = k with the sketch; A1 0 < k < 1 (four roots, all with x < 3); A1 k > 9 (two roots each side of x = 3).

parts.working: B1 eigenvalues are the entries of D; B1 third column of P.

parts.label: a

parts.working: B1 B1

parts.label: c

parts.working: B1 det A = det D = 2 × (−1) × 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The matrix A = (1 2 0; 0 3 1; 0 0 −1). Write down the eigenvalues of A.
parts.working: B1 diagonal entries of a triangular matrix.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find a corresponding eigenvector for each eigenvalue.
parts.answer: λ = 1: (1, 0, 0)ᵀ; λ = 3: (1, 1, 0)ᵀ; λ = −1: (1, −1, 4)ᵀ (or any non-zero multiples)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence find a matrix P and a diagonal matrix D such that A = PDP⁻¹.
parts.answer: P = (1 1 1; 0 1 −1; 0 0 4), D = diag(1, 3, −1) (columns of P in the same order as D)
parts.working: B1 P with eigenvectors as columns; B1 D matching order.

practice.stem: Matrices are written row by row, with rows separated by semicolons; for example (1 2; 3 4) has first row 1, 2 and second row 3, 4. Column vectors are written as (x, y, z)ᵀ.

parts.text: The matrix A = (2 1 0; 0 −1 3; 0 0 1). Find matrices P and D, where D is diagonal, such that A = PDP⁻¹.

parts.text: The matrix A = (1 k 2; 0 2 1; 0 0 4), where k is a constant, has (1, 1, 0)ᵀ as an eigenvector. Find k and the corresponding eigenvalue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find matrices P and D such that A = PDP⁻¹, where D is a diagonal matrix.

parts.label: c

parts.working: B1 λ² − 2λ for λ = 1, 2, 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two cities, Lahore and Karachi, are modelled as a closed system. Each year 20% of the residents of Lahore move to Karachi and 30% of the residents of Karachi move to Lahore; everyone else stays. If the populations (in millions) in a given year are the column vector (L, K)ᵀ, the populations a year later are T(L, K)ᵀ. Write down the matrix T.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The matrix A = (1 1 0; 0 2 1; 0 0 3). Find the characteristic equation of A in the form λ³ + aλ² + bλ + c = 0.

parts.text: Use the Cayley-Hamilton theorem to find A⁻¹.

parts.text: The matrix A = (1 1 1; 0 2 1; 0 0 −1). Find the characteristic equation of A and hence show that A³ = 2A² + A − 2I.
parts.working: M1 (1 − λ)(2 − λ)(−1 − λ) = 0; A1 expanded; A1 Cayley-Hamilton gives A³ − 2A² − A + 2I = 0 (AG).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find constants p, q and r such that A⁵ = pA² + qA + rI.
parts.working: M1 A⁴ = 2A³ + A² − 2A; A1 A⁴ = 5A² − 4I; M1 A⁵ = 5A³ − 4A; A1 10A² + A − 10I.
