parts.text: Find the acute angle between the planes 2x − y + 2z = 7 and x + 4y − z = 3, giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the acute angle between the line r = 2i − k + λ(3i + j − 2k) and the plane x − 2y + 2z = 5. Give your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.
parts.working:
M1: sin θ = |b·n| / (|b||n|) (or find the angle with the normal and subtract from 90°)
A1: |3 − 2 − 4| / (√14 × 3) = 3/(3√14)
A1: θ = 15.5°

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The lines l₁ and l₂ have equations
l₁: r = i − 2j + 3k + λ(2i + 2j + k)
l₂: r = 4j − k + μ(4i − j + k)
Show that l₁ and l₂ are skew.
parts.answer: Not parallel (directions not multiples) and the equations for a common point have no solution, so skew.
parts.working:
B1: directions not parallel
M1: 1 + 2λ = 4μ, −2 + 2λ = 4 − μ; solve λ = 23/10, μ = 7/5
A1: z-components then differ, so no intersection (or (a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂) ≠ 0)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the acute angle between the directions of l₁ and l₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line l: r = 2i + j − 3k + t(i + 2j + 2k) meets the plane Π: 3x − y + z = 4 at the point X. Find the coordinates of X.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the acute angle between l and Π.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sloping roof panel on a house in Murree is modelled as part of a plane through the points A(0, 0, 3), B(8, 0, 3) and C(4, 5, 6), in metres, where the z-axis is vertical and the ground is z = 0.
Find an equation of the plane of the roof panel in the form ax + by + cz = d.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the angle between the roof panel and the horizontal ground.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The planes Π₁: 2x + y + z = 3 and Π₂: x + ky − z = 5, where k is a constant, meet at an angle of 60°. Show that k satisfies k² − 4k + 4 = 0, and hence find k.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For this value of k, find a vector equation of the line of intersection of Π₁ and Π₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The planes Π₁: x − y + 2z = 3 and Π₂: 3x + y − z = 4 meet in the line l. Find a vector equation of l.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the acute angle between l and the plane Π₃: 2x + 2y + z = 9.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the point where the line r = i − 2j + 4k + λ(2i + 3j − k) meets the plane x + y + 2z = 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The line l has equation r = 3i + j − 2k + λ(2i + k) and the plane Π has equation x + 4y − 2z = 5. Show that l is parallel to Π and does not lie in Π.
parts.answer: b·n = 2 + 0 − 2 = 0, so l ∥ Π; the point (3, 1, −2) gives 3 + 4 + 4 = 11 ≠ 5, so l is not in Π.
parts.working:
M1: (2, 0, 1)·(1, 4, −2) = 0
A1: parallel
B1: (3, 1, −2) does not satisfy the plane equation (11 ≠ 5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance between l and Π.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find a vector equation of the line of intersection of the planes x + 2y + z = 4 and 2x − y + 3z = 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the point where this line meets the plane x + y + z = 6.
parts.working:
M1: substitute general point; t = 17/5
A1: (25, −2, −17)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The line l has equation r = i + pj + 2k + t(2i − j + k), where p is a constant, and the plane Π₁ has equation x + 3y + z = 9.
Show that l is parallel to Π₁ for every value of p.
parts.working: B1: direction · normal = 2 − 3 + 1 = 0

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of p for which l lies in Π₁.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For the value of p found in (b), the plane Π₂ contains l and is perpendicular to Π₁. Find the Cartesian equation of Π₂.
parts.working:
M1: normal of Π₂ is perpendicular to both (2, −1, 1) and (1, 3, 1)
A1: (2, −1, 1) × (1, 3, 1) = (−4, −1, 7)
A1: through (1, 2, 2): 4x + y − 7z = −8

parts.label: d
parts.text: For p = 5, find the distance between l and Π₁.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation x³ + xy + y² = 7. Show that the point (1, 2) lies on C and find dy/dx at this point.
parts.working: B1 verification; M1 3x² + y + x(dy/dx) + 2y(dy/dx) = 0; A1 dy/dx = −(3x² + y)/(x + 2y) = −5/5 = −1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the equation of the tangent to C at (1, 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation x²y + y² = 6. Find dy/dx in terms of x and y.
parts.working: M1 product rule on x²y; M1 2xy + x²(dy/dx) + 2y(dy/dx) = 0; A1 result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the equation of the tangent to C at the point (1, 2), giving your answer in the form ax + by = c.
parts.working: M1 gradient −4/5; A1 4x + 5y = 14.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation xeʸ + y = 2. Find the gradient of C at the point where it crosses the x-axis.
parts.working: B1 y = 0 gives x = 2; M1 eʸ + xeʸ(dy/dx) + dy/dx = 0; A1 dy/dx = −eʸ/(xeʸ + 1) = −1/3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the equation of the normal to C at this point.
parts.working: M1 normal gradient 3; A1 y = 3(x − 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation x² + xy + y² = 7. Find the value of dy/dx at the point (1, 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of d²y/dx² at (1, 2).
parts.working: M1 differentiate the implicit equation again: 2 + 2(dy/dx) + x(d²y/dx²) + 2(dy/dx)² + 2y(d²y/dx²) = 0; M1 substitute x = 1, y = 2, dy/dx = −4/5; A1 5(d²y/dx²) = −(2 − 8/5 + 32/25) = −42/25; A1 d²y/dx² = −42/125.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation e^(xy) = x + y. Show that (0, 1) lies on C and that dy/dx = 0 there.
parts.working: B1 verification; M1 e^(xy)(y + x(dy/dx)) = 1 + dy/dx; A1 at (0, 1): 1 = 1 + dy/dx so dy/dx = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find d²y/dx² at (0, 1) and hence determine the nature of this stationary point.
parts.working: M1 differentiate again: e^(xy)(y + x y′)² + e^(xy)(2y′ + x y″) = y″; M1 substitute x = 0, y = 1, y′ = 0; A1 y″ = 1; A1 positive, so a minimum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation sin x + sin y = 1, for 0 < x < π/2, 0 < y < π/2. Find dy/dx at the point (π/6, π/6).
parts.working: M1 cos x + cos y(dy/dx) = 0; A1 dy/dx = −cos x/cos y = −1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that d²y/dx² at (π/6, π/6) is 2√3/3.
parts.working: M1 differentiate cos x + cos y·y′ = 0 again: −sin x − sin y·(y′)² + cos y·y″ = 0; M1 substitute values; A1 (√3/2)y″ = 1/2 + 1/2; A1 y″ = 2/√3 = 2√3/3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y³ + 3x²y = 4. Show that dy/dx = −2xy/(x² + y²).
parts.working: M1 3y²(dy/dx) + 6xy + 3x²(dy/dx) = 0; M1 collect terms; A1 result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find dy/dx and d²y/dx² at the point (1, 1), and describe what this suggests about the curve near this point.
parts.answer: dy/dx = −1, d²y/dx² = 0; the curve is approximately straight there (possible point of inflection)
parts.working: B1 dy/dx = −1; M1 differentiate (x² + y²)y′ = −2xy: (2x + 2y y′)y′ + (x² + y²)y″ = −2y − 2x y′; M1 substitute: (2 − 2)(−1) + 2y″ = −2 + 2; A1 y″ = 0, with comment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation x² + xy + y² = 12. Find the coordinates of the points on C at which the tangent is parallel to the x-axis.
parts.working: M1 dy/dx = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y); M1 dy/dx = 0 gives y = −2x; M1 substitute: 3x² = 12; A1 (2, −4) and (−2, 4).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use d²y/dx² to determine the nature of each of these points.
parts.answer: (2, −4) is a minimum (d²y/dx² = 1/3); (−2, 4) is a maximum (d²y/dx² = −1/3)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the points on C at which the tangent is parallel to the y-axis.
parts.working: M1 x + 2y = 0; A1 both points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation x³ + y³ = 6xy. Find the exact coordinates of the point on C, other than the origin, at which the tangent is parallel to the x-axis.
parts.working: M1 3x² + 3y²(dy/dx) = 6y + 6x(dy/dx); A1 dy/dx = (2y − x²)/(y² − 2x); M1 dy/dx = 0 gives y = x²/2; M1 substitute: x³ + x⁶/8 = 3x³, x³ = 16; A1 x = 2∛2, y = 2∛4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that at this point d²y/dx² = −1.
parts.working: M1 differentiate x² + y²y′ = 2y + 2xy′ again: 2x + 2y(y′)² + y²y″ = 4y′ + 2xy″; A1 with y′ = 0: y″ = −2x/(y² − 2x); A1 y² − 2x = 2^(10/3) − 2^(7/3) = 2^(7/3) = 2x, so y″ = −1 (a maximum).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A curve is defined parametrically by x = t² + 1, y = t³ − 3t. Find dy/dx in terms of t.
parts.working: M1 (dy/dt)/(dx/dt); A1 result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An ellipse has parametric equations x = 2 cos θ, y = 3 sin θ. Find dy/dx in terms of θ.
parts.answer: dy/dx = −3 cos θ/(2 sin θ) = −(3/2) cot θ
parts.working: M1 dy/dθ = 3 cos θ, dx/dθ = −2 sin θ; A1 result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the equation of the tangent to the ellipse at the point where θ = π/4, giving your answer in the form ax + by = c√2.
parts.working: M1 point (√2, 3√2/2); M1 gradient −3/2; A1 3x + 2y = 6√2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A curve has parametric equations x = 3t − 1, y = 2/t, t ≠ 0. Find dy/dx in terms of t.
parts.working: M1 dy/dt = −2/t², dx/dt = 3; A1 −2/(3t²).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the equation of the normal to the curve at the point where t = 1.
parts.working: B1 point (2, 2); M1 normal gradient 3/2; A1 y − 2 = (3/2)(x − 2), i.e. 2y = 3x − 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A curve has parametric equations x = t + 1/t, y = t − 1/t, t > 1. Show that dy/dx = (t² + 1)/(t² − 1).
parts.working: M1 dx/dt = 1 − 1/t², dy/dt = 1 + 1/t²; A1 multiply through by t².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that d²y/dx² = −4t³/(t² − 1)³ and find its value when t = 2.
parts.working: M1 d/dt of dy/dx = −4t/(t² − 1)²; M1 divide by dx/dt = (t² − 1)/t²; A1 −4t³/(t² − 1)³; A1 −32/27.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A curve has parametric equations x = ln(1 + t²), y = 2 tan⁻¹ t, for t > 0. Show that dy/dx = 1/t.
parts.working: M1 dx/dt = 2t/(1 + t²), dy/dt = 2/(1 + t²); A1 dy/dx = 1/t.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find d²y/dx² in terms of t, and its value at the point where t = 1.
parts.working: M1 d/dt(1/t) = −1/t²; M1 divide by 2t/(1 + t²); A1 −(1 + t²)/(2t³) = −1 at t = 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A curve has parametric equations x = eᵗ cos t, y = eᵗ sin t. Show that dy/dx = (sin t + cos t)/(cos t − sin t).
parts.working: M1 product rule for both; A1 eᵗ cancels.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that d²y/dx² = 2/(eᵗ(cos t − sin t)³) and find its value at t = 0.
parts.working: M1 quotient rule in t: numerator (cos t − sin t)² + (sin t + cos t)² = 2; A1 d/dt = 2/(cos t − sin t)²; M1 divide by eᵗ(cos t − sin t); A1 value 2 at t = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A curve has parametric equations x = t² + 2t, y = t³ − 12t. Find the values of t at the stationary points of the curve.
parts.working: M1 dy/dt = 3t² − 12 = 0; A1 t = ±2 (dx/dt ≠ 0 there).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find d²y/dx² in terms of t.
parts.working: M1 dy/dx = (3t² − 12)/(2t + 2); M1 differentiate w.r.t. t and divide by dx/dt; A1 result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the stationary points and determine their nature.
parts.working: A1 (8, −16) with 1/3 > 0, minimum; A1 (0, 16) with −3 < 0, maximum; B1 correct coordinates for both.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cycloid traced by a point on the rim of a bicycle wheel of radius a has parametric equations x = a(θ − sin θ), y = a(1 − cos θ), for 0 < θ < 2π. Show that dy/dx = cot(θ/2).
parts.working: M1 dy/dx = sin θ/(1 − cos θ); M1 double-angle forms 2 sin(θ/2)cos(θ/2)/(2 sin²(θ/2)); A1 cot(θ/2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that d²y/dx² = −1/(4a sin⁴(θ/2)), and deduce that d²y/dx² = −a/y².
parts.working: M1 d/dθ cot(θ/2) = −(1/2)cosec²(θ/2); M1 divide by a(1 − cos θ) = 2a sin²(θ/2); A1 −1/(4a sin⁴(θ/2)); A1 y = 2a sin²(θ/2) so y² = 4a² sin⁴(θ/2), giving −a/y².

parts.label: a
parts.text: A curve has parametric equations x = t², y = t³. Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point P where t = 1.
parts.working: M1 dy/dx = 3t/2; A1 gradient 3/2 at (1, 1); A1 2y = 3x − 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The tangent at P meets the curve again at Q. Find the coordinates of Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the Maclaurin series for ln(1 + sin x) up to and including the term in x³.
parts.working: M1 f′ = cos x/(1 + sin x), f′(0) = 1; M1 f″ = −1/(1 + sin x), f″(0) = −1; M1 f‴ = cos x/(1 + sin x)², f‴(0) = 1; M1 f(0) = 0 and use of Maclaurin formula; A1 x − x²/2 + x³/6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use differentiation to find the Maclaurin series for eˣ cos x up to and including the term in x³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your series to find an approximation to e^0.1 cos 0.1, giving your answer to 5 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that f(x) = sec x, show that f″(x) = 2 sec³x − sec x.
parts.working: M1 f′ = sec x tan x; M1 f″ = sec x tan²x + sec³x; A1 use tan²x = sec²x − 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the Maclaurin series for sec x up to and including the term in x⁴.
parts.working: M1 f‴ = 6 sec³x tan x − sec x tan x, f‴(0) = 0; M1 f⁗ = 18 sec³x tan²x + 6 sec⁵x − sec x tan²x − sec³x, f⁗(0) = 5; A1 f(0) = 1, f″(0) = 1; A1 1 + x²/2 + 5x⁴/24.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the Maclaurin series for tan⁻¹(1 + x) up to and including the term in x³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the Maclaurin series for eˣ√(1 + 2x) up to and including the term in x³.
parts.working: M1 √(1 + 2x) = 1 + x − x²/2 + x³/2 + … (or differentiate directly); M1 multiply by 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6; A1 x term 2x; A1 x² term 1/2 + 1 − 1/2 = 1; A1 x³ term 1/2 − 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your series to estimate e^0.1 √1.2 correct to 6 decimal places, and find the percentage error of your estimate correct to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given f(x) = ln(cos x), for −π/2 < x < π/2, find the Maclaurin series for f(x) up to and including the term in x⁴.
parts.working: M1 f′ = −tan x, f″ = −sec²x, f‴ = −2 sec²x tan x; M1 f⁗ = −4 sec²x tan²x − 2 sec⁴x; A1 f(0) = 0, f′(0) = 0, f″(0) = −1, f‴(0) = 0, f⁗(0) = −2; M1 Maclaurin formula; A1 −x²/2 − 2x⁴/24; A1 = −x²/2 − x⁴/12.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence, without further differentiation, find the Maclaurin series for tan x up to and including the term in x³.
parts.working: M1 tan x = −d/dx ln(cos x); A1 −(−x − x³/3) = x + x³/3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that y = sin⁻¹x, show that (1 − x²)(d²y/dx²) − x(dy/dx) = 0.
parts.working: M1 dy/dx = (1 − x²)^(−1/2), so √(1 − x²)·dy/dx = 1; M1 differentiate: √(1 − x²)y″ − x(1 − x²)^(−1/2)y′ = 0; A1 multiply by √(1 − x²).

parts.label: b
parts.text: By differentiating this result three more times, find the Maclaurin series for sin⁻¹x up to and including the term in x⁵.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find dy/dx when y = sinh⁻¹(3x).
parts.working: M1 chain rule with d/du sinh⁻¹u = 1/√(u² + 1); A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find dy/dx when y = cosh(x²).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find dy/dx when y = tanh⁻¹(x/2), for |x| < 2, simplifying your answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Differentiate y = x² tanh 3x with respect to x.
parts.working: M1 product rule; A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact gradient of the curve y = cos⁻¹(x/2) at the point where x = 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By writing x = cosh y, prove that d/dx (cosh⁻¹x) = 1/√(x² − 1), for x > 1.
parts.working: M1 dx/dy = sinh y; M1 sinh y = √(cosh²y − 1) = √(x² − 1) (positive since y > 0); A1 dy/dx = 1/√(x² − 1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the gradient of the curve y = x cosh⁻¹x at the point where x = 2, giving your answer in exact form and correct to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: M1 product rule: cosh⁻¹x + x/√(x² − 1); M1 cosh⁻¹2 = ln(2 + √3); A1 ln(2 + √3) + 2√3/3 = 2.472.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that d/dx [tan⁻¹(eˣ)] = (1/2) sech x.
parts.working: M1 chain rule: eˣ/(1 + e²ˣ); M1 divide numerator and denominator by eˣ: 1/(e⁻ˣ + eˣ); A1 = 1/(2 cosh x) = (1/2) sech x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of ∫₀^(ln 3) sech x dx.
parts.working: M1 ∫ sech x dx = 2 tan⁻¹(eˣ); M1 limits: 2 tan⁻¹3 − 2 tan⁻¹1; A1 2 tan⁻¹3 − π/2 ≈ 0.927.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The curve C has equation y = 3 cosh x − sinh x. Show that C has exactly one stationary point and find its exact coordinates.
parts.working: M1 dy/dx = 3 sinh x − cosh x = 0; M1 tanh x = 1/3 (only one solution since tanh is one-one); M1 x = tanh⁻¹(1/3) = ½ ln((1 + 1/3)/(1 − 1/3)) = ½ ln 2; M1 cosh x = 3/(2√2), sinh x = 1/(2√2); A1 y = 9/(2√2) − 1/(2√2) = 2√2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the nature of the stationary point.
parts.working: M1 d²y/dx² = 3 cosh x − sinh x = y; A1 at the point d²y/dx² = 2√2 > 0, so a minimum.

practice.stem: Matrices are written row by row, with rows separated by semicolons; for example (1 2; 3 4) has first row 1, 2 and second row 3, 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The matrix M = (3 1; 2 2) represents a transformation T of the x-y plane. Find the equations of the invariant lines of T that pass through the origin.
parts.working: M1 image of (x, mx) is (3x + mx, 2x + 2mx); M1 2 + 2m = m(3 + m); A1 m² + m − 2 = 0; A1 m = 1 or m = −2, so y = x and y = −2x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the image of the point (2, 2) under T. Hence state the factor by which T multiplies the distance from the origin of each point on y = x.

practice.stem: Matrices are written row by row, with rows separated by semicolons; for example (1 2; 3 4) has first row 1, 2 and second row 3, 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The transformation S of the plane is represented by the matrix (1 4; 1 1). Find the invariant lines of S through the origin, giving your answers in the form y = mx.
parts.working: M1 image of (x, mx) is (x + 4mx, x + mx); M1 1 + m = m(1 + 4m); A1 4m² = 1; A1 m = ±½.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the line x = 0 is not invariant under S.
parts.working: B1 (0, 1) maps to (4, 1), which is not on x = 0.

practice.stem: Matrices are written row by row, with rows separated by semicolons; for example (1 2; 3 4) has first row 1, 2 and second row 3, 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The matrix M = (3 −2; 1 0) represents the transformation T. Show that every point on the line y = x is an invariant point of T.
parts.working: M1 M(t, t)ᵀ = (3t − 2t, t)ᵀ; A1 = (t, t)ᵀ for all t.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the equation of the other invariant line of T through the origin.
parts.working: M1 image of (x, mx) is ((3 − 2m)x, x); M1 1 = m(3 − 2m) gives 2m² − 3m + 1 = 0; A1 m = 1 (already found) or m = ½: y = ½x.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the points on the line in part (b) are not invariant points.
parts.answer: (2, 1) maps to (4, 2): the line maps to itself but each point moves (distances from O are doubled).

practice.stem: Matrices are written row by row, with rows separated by semicolons; for example (1 2; 3 4) has first row 1, 2 and second row 3, 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The transformation T is a reflection in the x-axis followed by a stretch, scale factor 3, parallel to the y-axis. Find the matrix M that represents T.
parts.working: M1 stretch × reflection: (1 0; 0 3)(1 0; 0 −1); A1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the invariant points of T and the invariant lines of T through the origin.
parts.answer: Invariant points: the x-axis; invariant lines through O: y = 0 and x = 0
parts.working: B1 points with −3y = y, i.e. y = 0; B1 y = 0; B1 x = 0 (as (0, y) maps to (0, −3y)).

practice.stem: Matrices are written row by row, with rows separated by semicolons; for example (1 2; 3 4) has first row 1, 2 and second row 3, 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The transformation H is represented by the matrix (1 3; 0 1). Describe H fully.
parts.answer: Shear with the x-axis invariant, (x, y) → (x + 3y, y)
parts.working: B1 shear; B1 x-axis invariant and e.g. (0, 1) maps to (3, 1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the invariant points of H.
parts.working: B1 (x + 3y, y) = (x, y) requires y = 0.

parts.label: c

parts.text: Find the probability that a customer waits between 3 and 8 minutes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Given that a customer has already waited 5 minutes, find the probability that they wait at least 3 more minutes.

practice.stem: The continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = kx² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, f(x) = c for 1 < x ≤ 3 and f(x) = 0 otherwise, where k and c are constants. The function f is continuous at x = 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that k = 3/7.
parts.working: M1 continuity at x = 1 gives c = k; M1 ∫₀¹ kx² dx + ∫₁³ k dx = k/3 + 2k; A1 7k/3 = 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the cumulative distribution function of X.
parts.answer: F(x) = 0 for x < 0; x³/7 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1; (3x − 2)/7 for 1 < x ≤ 3; 1 for x > 3
parts.working: M1 ∫₀ˣ 3t²/7 dt; A1 x³/7; M1 1/7 + 3(x − 1)/7; A1 (3x − 2)/7, with 0 and 1 outside.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find P(0.5 < X < 2).

practice.stem: A dart lands at a random point on a circular board of radius 20 cm, every point of the board being equally likely. R cm is the distance of the point from the centre of the board.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that P(R ≤ r) = r²/400 for 0 ≤ r ≤ 20, and hence find the probability density function of R.
parts.working: M1 probability = area of circle radius r ÷ area of board = πr²/(π × 20²); A1 r²/400; B1 differentiate: r/200.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find E(R).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability that the dart lands between 10 cm and 15 cm from the centre.

practice.stem: The continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = x/8 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4, and f(x) = 0 otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the cumulative distribution function of X for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4.
parts.working: M1 ∫₀ˣ t/8 dt; A1 x²/16.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the median of X in exact form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the 90th percentile of X.

practice.stem: The time, T minutes, taken by a student to solve a daily puzzle has probability density function f(t) = 3t²/64 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4, and f(t) = 0 otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the median of the time taken.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the interquartile range of the time taken.
parts.working: M1 upper quartile t³ = 48, t = 3.634; M1 lower quartile t³ = 16, t = 2.520; A1 IQR = 1.11 minutes.

practice.stem:
The continuous random variable X has cumulative distribution function
F(x) = 0 for x < 0,
F(x) = x²/20 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2,
F(x) = (20x − x² − 20)/80 for 2 < x ≤ 10,
F(x) = 1 for x > 10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the median, m, of X satisfies m² − 20m + 60 = 0, and hence find m in exact form.
parts.working: M1 F(2) = 1/5 < 1/2, so the median is in 2 < x ≤ 10; M1 (20m − m² − 20)/80 = 1/2; A1 m² − 20m + 60 = 0; A1 m = 10 − √40 = 10 − 2√10 (the other root exceeds 10).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the interquartile range of X, correct to 3 significant figures.

practice.stem: The length, L minutes, of a call to a customer help line in Faisalabad has cumulative distribution function F(l) = 1 − e^(−0.25l) for l ≥ 0, and F(l) = 0 for l < 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the median call length, in exact form and correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The longest 10% of calls are checked by a supervisor. Find the shortest call length that is checked.

practice.stem: The continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = k(4x − x³) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, and f(x) = 0 otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the value of k.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the median m satisfies m⁴ − 8m² + 8 = 0, and hence find m correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 F(x) = x²/2 − x⁴/16; M1 m²/2 − m⁴/16 = 1/2; A1 m⁴ − 8m² + 8 = 0; A1 m² = 4 − 2√2 (other root gives m > 2), m = 1.08.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find E(X) and hence state, with a reason, whether the distribution is positively or negatively skewed.
parts.answer: E(X) = 16/15; mean < median so negatively skewed
parts.working: M1 (1/4)∫₀² (4x² − x⁴) dx; A1 16/15 = 1.067; B1 mean < median (1.082), so negative skew.

practice.stem: The value, X million rupees, of a claim on a house insurance policy has probability density function f(x) = 4/x⁵ for x ≥ 1, and f(x) = 0 otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the median value of a claim, in exact form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The insurer sends the largest 5% of claims for extra checks. Find the smallest claim value that is checked.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability that a claim is greater than the mean claim value.

practice.stem: The continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = 2/(x + 1)² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, and f(x) = 0 otherwise. Its cumulative distribution function is F(x).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that F(x) = 2x/(x + 1) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the median and the interquartile range of X.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find E(X) in exact form and compare it with the median.
parts.working: M1 ∫₀¹ 2x/(x + 1)² dx = 2∫₀¹ (1/(x + 1) − 1/(x + 1)²) dx; A1 2 ln 2 − 1 = 0.386; B1 greater than the median 1/3 (positive skew).

practice.stem: The continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = x/2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, and f(x) = 0 otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the cumulative distribution function of X.
parts.working: B1 ∫₀ˣ t/2 dt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The random variable Y is defined by Y = X². Find the cumulative distribution function of Y, and hence identify the distribution of Y.
parts.answer: G(y) = y/4 for 0 ≤ y ≤ 4; Y is uniformly distributed on [0, 4] with pdf 1/4
parts.working: M1 G(y) = P(X² ≤ y) = P(X ≤ √y); M1 = F(√y); A1 y/4 for 0 ≤ y ≤ 4; A1 pdf g(y) = 1/4, so Y is uniform on [0, 4].

practice.stem: The continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = 3x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, and f(x) = 0 otherwise. The random variable Y is defined by Y = 2X + 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the cumulative distribution function of Y.
parts.answer: G(y) = ((y − 1)/2)³ for 1 ≤ y ≤ 3 (0 for y < 1, 1 for y > 3)
parts.working: M1 G(y) = P(2X + 1 ≤ y) = P(X ≤ (y − 1)/2); M1 F(x) = x³; A1 ((y − 1)/2)³ with range 1 ≤ y ≤ 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the probability density function of Y, and find E(Y).

practice.stem: The continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = 3/(2x²) for 1 ≤ x ≤ 3, and f(x) = 0 otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the cumulative distribution function of X.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The random variable Y = 1/X. Show that the cumulative distribution function of Y is G(y) = (3y − 1)/2 for 1/3 ≤ y ≤ 1, and identify the distribution of Y.
parts.answer: Y is uniform on [1/3, 1], with pdf 3/2

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence write down E(Y).
parts.working: B1 midpoint of [1/3, 1].

practice.stem: The continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, and f(x) = 0 otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability density function of Y, where Y = √X.
parts.working: M1 G(y) = P(√X ≤ y) = P(X ≤ y²); M1 F(x) = x² so G(y) = y⁴; A1 for 0 ≤ y ≤ 1; A1 g(y) = 4y³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find E(Y) and the median of Y.
parts.working: M1 ∫₀¹ 4y⁴ dy; A1 4/5; B1 y⁴ = 1/2 gives 0.841.

practice.stem: The random variable X is uniformly distributed on the interval [0, 4], so its probability density function is 1/4 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4. The random variable Y is defined by Y = (X − 2)².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that, for 0 ≤ y ≤ 4, P(Y ≤ y) = √y/2.
parts.working: M1 P((X − 2)² ≤ y) = P(2 − √y ≤ X ≤ 2 + √y); M1 = (2√y)/4 using the uniform pdf 1/4; A1 √y/2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability density function of Y and use it to find E(Y).
parts.working: M1 differentiate; A1 1/(4√y); A1 ∫₀⁴ √y/4 dy = (1/6)(8) = 4/3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why your answer to part (b) is equal to Var(X).
parts.working: B1 Var(X) = E((X − μ)²) with μ = 2, and Var(X) = 4²/12 = 4/3.

practice.stem: The continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = 2e^(−2x) for x ≥ 0, and f(x) = 0 otherwise. The random variable Y is defined by Y = e^X.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the cumulative distribution function of Y is G(y) = 1 − 1/y² for y ≥ 1.
parts.working: M1 F(x) = 1 − e^(−2x); M1 G(y) = P(e^X ≤ y) = P(X ≤ ln y); M1 = 1 − e^(−2 ln y); A1 1 − y⁻², for y ≥ 1 since X ≥ 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability density function of Y, and find E(Y) and the median of Y.
parts.working: B1 2y⁻³; M1 E(Y) = ∫₁^∞ 2y⁻² dy; A1 2; B1 1 − m⁻² = 1/2 gives m = √2.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A clinic in Rawalpindi records the systolic blood pressure (mm Hg) of 8 adults before and after a 6-week walking programme.
Patient: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
Before: 142, 156, 138, 149, 161, 147, 152, 158
After: 137, 148, 139, 141, 150, 146, 145, 160
Use a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, at the 5% significance level, to test whether the programme reduces median blood pressure.
parts.answer: T = 4.5; critical value 5; reject H₀: evidence that the median blood pressure is reduced
parts.working: B1 H₀: population median difference (before − after) = 0, H₁: > 0; M1 differences 5, 8, −1, 8, 11, 1, 7, −2; M1 rank |differences|: −1→1.5, 1→1.5, −2→3, 5→4, 7→5, 8→6.5, 8→6.5, 11→8; A1 P = 31.5, Q = 4.5; A1 T = 4.5; B1 one-tailed 5% critical value for n = 8 is 5; A1 4.5 ≤ 5, reject H₀; there is evidence that the programme reduces median blood pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bakery in Karachi claims that the median mass of its naan is 50 g. A random sample of 10 naan has masses (g):
47.2, 51.8, 44.9, 53.6, 49.1, 42.3, 55.4, 46.7, 48.5, 43.1
Test the claim using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test at the 5% significance level.
parts.answer: T = 17; critical value 8; do not reject H₀: no evidence against the claim
parts.working: B1 H₀: median = 50, H₁: median ≠ 50; M1 differences from 50; M1 ranks: −0.9→1, −1.5→2, 1.8→3, −2.8→4, −3.3→5, 3.6→6, −5.1→7, 5.4→8, −6.9→9, −7.7→10; A1 P = 17, Q = 38; A1 T = 17; B1 two-tailed 5% critical value 8; A1 do not reject H₀; insufficient evidence that the median differs from 50 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State an assumption needed for this test to be valid.
parts.answer: The masses come from a population whose distribution is symmetric (about the median)
parts.working: B1 symmetric distribution (random sample also acceptable as additional).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A Wilcoxon signed-rank test is carried out on 13 paired observations. One pair has a zero difference. The sum of the ranks of the positive differences is 61. Find the value of the test statistic T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Carry out the test at the 5% significance level, using a two-tailed alternative, stating your hypotheses.
parts.answer: Critical value 13; do not reject H₀
parts.working: B1 H₀: median difference 0, H₁: median difference ≠ 0; B1 critical value 13; A1 17 > 13: do not reject H₀; insufficient evidence of a difference in medians.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Seven students in Kuala Lumpur sit a mental-arithmetic quiz, then practise for a week and sit a similar quiz. Their scores are:
First quiz: 64, 71, 58, 80, 67, 75, 62
Second quiz: 70, 74, 57, 88, 73, 84, 68
State suitable hypotheses for a test of whether practice increases the median score.
parts.answer: H₀: median of (second − first) = 0; H₁: median of (second − first) > 0
parts.working: B1 both, in terms of the population median difference.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Carry out a Wilcoxon signed-rank test at the 5% significance level.
parts.answer: T = 1; critical value 3; reject H₀: evidence that practice increases the median score
parts.working: M1 differences (second − first): 6, 3, −1, 8, 6, 9, 6; M1 ranks: −1→1, 3→2, 6→4, 6→4, 6→4, 8→6, 9→7; A1 P = 27, Q = 1, T = 1; B1 critical value 3; A1 conclusion in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Ten table-tennis players at a club in Islamabad each have their reaction time (seconds) measured before and after a caffeine-free energy drink.
Player: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J
Before: 0.42, 0.38, 0.51, 0.47, 0.36, 0.44, 0.49, 0.40, 0.45, 0.53
After: 0.39, 0.38, 0.45, 0.48, 0.30, 0.37, 0.41, 0.42, 0.44, 0.44
Test at the 5% significance level whether the drink reduces median reaction time.
parts.answer: n = 9 (one zero discarded); T = 4.5; critical value 8; reject H₀: evidence of a reduction
parts.working: B1 H₀: median difference (before − after) = 0, H₁: > 0; M1 differences, discarding the zero (player B), n = 9; M1 ranks: −0.01→1.5, 0.01→1.5, −0.02→3, 0.03→4, 0.06→5.5, 0.06→5.5, 0.07→7, 0.08→8, 0.09→9; A1 P = 40.5, Q = 4.5; A1 T = 4.5; B1 critical value 8; A1 reject H₀; evidence that the drink reduces median reaction time.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A soil scientist in Faisalabad believes that the median pH of soil in a district is greater than 7.5. She measures 12 randomly chosen samples:
6.8, 7.9, 8.4, 7.1, 8.4, 9.2, 6.5, 8.7, 7.6, 9.0, 8.1, 7.4
Use a Wilcoxon signed-rank test at the 2.5% significance level to test her belief. (Give tied absolute differences the mean of their ranks.)
parts.answer: T = 20; critical value 13; do not reject H₀: insufficient evidence that the median pH exceeds 7.5
parts.working: B1 H₀: median = 7.5, H₁: median > 7.5; M1 differences from 7.5; M1 ranks with ties averaged: 0.1→1.5, −0.1→1.5, 0.4→3.5, −0.4→3.5, 0.6→5, −0.7→6, 0.9→7.5, 0.9→7.5, −1→9, 1.2→10, 1.5→11, 1.7→12; A1 P = 58; A1 Q = 20, T = 20; B1 critical value for n = 12 at 2.5% one-tailed: 13; M1 comparison; A1 conclusion in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A Wilcoxon signed-rank test compares the times taken by 30 delivery riders in Lahore to complete a route using an old map app and a new one (old time − new time). There are no zero differences. The sum of the ranks of the positive differences is 314. Using a suitable normal approximation, test at the 5% significance level whether the new app reduces the median time.
parts.answer: T = 151; z = −1.666; reject H₀: evidence that the new app reduces median time
parts.working: B1 H₀: median difference 0, H₁: median difference > 0; M1 Q = 465 − 314 = 151, T = 151; B1 E(T) = 30 × 31/4 = 232.5, Var(T) = 30 × 31 × 61/24 = 2363.75; M1 z = (151 + 0.5 − 232.5)/√2363.75 with continuity correction; A1 z = −1.666; M1 compare with −1.645; A1 reject H₀; evidence that the new app reduces median time.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A phone maker claims that the median battery life of its new model under a standard test is 20 hours. A consumer group in Dubai tests 14 phones and records (hours):
18.6, 21.4, 17.9, 19.2, 16.8, 20.3, 18.1, 15.7, 19.6, 17.4, 16.2, 18.9, 20.8, 17.1
Test, at the 1% significance level, whether the median battery life is less than claimed.
parts.answer: T = 11; critical value 15; reject H₀: evidence that the median is less than 20 hours
parts.working: B1 H₀: median = 20, H₁: median < 20; M1 differences from 20; M1 ranks: 0.3→1, −0.4→2, −0.8→3.5, 0.8→3.5, −1.1→5, −1.4→6.5, 1.4→6.5, −1.9→8, −2.1→9, −2.6→10, −2.9→11, −3.2→12, −3.8→13, −4.3→14; A1 P = 11, Q = 94; A1 T = 11; B1 1% one-tailed critical value for n = 14: 15; A1 reject H₀; strong evidence that the median battery life is below 20 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An agricultural station near Multan divides each of 9 fields into two halves. One half is sown with wheat variety X and the other with variety Y. The yields (tonnes per hectare) are:
Field: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9
X: 3.42, 2.98, 3.75, 3.10, 3.56, 2.87, 3.33, 3.64, 3.05
Y: 3.51, 3.12, 3.69, 3.30, 3.71, 3.04, 3.29, 3.88, 3.27
Test at the 10% significance level whether there is a difference between the median yields of the two varieties.
parts.answer: T = 3; critical value 8; reject H₀: evidence of a difference
parts.working: B1 H₀: median difference = 0, H₁: ≠ 0; M1 differences X − Y; M1 ranks: 0.04→1, 0.06→2, −0.09→3, −0.14→4, −0.15→5, −0.17→6, −0.2→7, −0.22→8, −0.24→9; A1 P = 3, Q = 42; A1 T = 3; B1 two-tailed 10% critical value for n = 9: 8; A1 reject H₀; evidence of a difference in median yields.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a paired test is appropriate here.
parts.answer: Each field gives a natural pair, removing differences between fields (soil, water)
parts.working: B1 same field for both varieties, so field-to-field variation is controlled.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two examiners each mark the same 14 essays out of 100.
Examiner 1: 56, 72, 64, 81, 49, 68, 77, 59, 85, 62, 70, 53, 66, 74
Examiner 2: 61, 70, 71, 84, 57, 66, 83, 68, 86, 70, 79, 50, 75, 78
Use a Wilcoxon signed-rank test at the 2% significance level to test whether there is a difference between the examiners' median marks. Use the mean rank for tied values.
parts.answer: T = 9.5; critical value 15; reject H₀: evidence of a difference between the examiners
parts.working: B1 H₀: median difference = 0, H₁: ≠ 0; M1 differences (E1 − E2); M1 ranks with ties: −1→1, 2→2.5, 2→2.5, −3→4.5, 3→4.5, −4→6, −5→7, −6→8, −7→9, −8→10.5, −8→10.5, −9→13, −9→13, −9→13; A1 P = 9.5; A1 Q = 95.5; B1 2% two-tailed critical value for n = 14 is 15; M1 T = 9.5 compared; A1 reject H₀; evidence that the examiners differ (examiner 2 tends to mark higher).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a Wilcoxon signed-rank test with 15 non-zero differences, P denotes the sum of the ranks of the positive differences. Find the set of values of P for which H₀: median difference = 0 is rejected in favour of H₁: median difference ≠ 0 at the 5% significance level.
parts.working: B1 P + Q = 120; B1 critical value 25; M1 reject when min(P, 120 − P) ≤ 25; A1 P ≤ 25 or P ≥ 95.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The experimenter actually obtains P = 96. One difference, with rank 7, was later found to have been recorded with the wrong sign: it should have been negative, not positive. Determine whether the conclusion of the test changes.
parts.answer: Yes: corrected P = 89, so H₀ is no longer rejected
parts.working: M1 corrected P = 96 − 7 = 89, Q = 31; A1 T = 31 > 25; A1 originally T = 24 ≤ 25 (reject), now do not reject: conclusion changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A Wilcoxon signed-rank test is to be carried out on 40 non-zero paired differences, using a one-tailed test at the 1% significance level and a normal approximation with continuity correction. State the mean and variance of the test statistic T under H₀.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the largest value of T that leads to rejection of H₀.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A Wilcoxon signed-rank test is used to test H₀: median = 12 against H₁: median ≠ 12 for the data
12.4, 15.1, 11.2, 13.8, 10.6, 14.3, 9.9
Show that, for these 7 values, P = 18 and Q = 10, and carry out the test at the 5% significance level.
parts.answer: T = 10; critical value 2; do not reject H₀

parts.label: b
parts.text: An eighth value x is added, where x > 16. Find the new value of T and determine whether the conclusion changes.
parts.answer: T = 10; critical value 3; conclusion unchanged: do not reject H₀
parts.working: M1 x − 12 > 4 has the largest absolute difference, rank 8, others keep their ranks; A1 P = 26, Q = 10, T = 10; A1 critical value for n = 8 is 3: do not reject H₀; conclusion unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Researchers in Nairobi compare the daily water use (litres) of 27 households before and after fitting water-saving taps (before − after). One household shows no change. The sum of the ranks of the negative differences is 98. Find the test statistic and, using a normal approximation with continuity correction, find the p-value for a test of H₀: median difference = 0 against H₁: median difference > 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the conclusion at the 1% significance level.
parts.working: B1 comparison and conclusion in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A tea company in Lahore asks 12 randomly chosen customers to taste its usual blend and a new blend. 9 prefer the new blend and 3 prefer the usual one. Use a sign test at the 5% significance level to test whether customers in general prefer the new blend.
parts.answer: P(X ≥ 9) = 0.0730; do not reject H₀: insufficient evidence of a preference
parts.working: B1 H₀: p = 0.5, H₁: p > 0.5, where p is the probability a customer prefers the new blend; M1 X ~ B(12, 0.5); M1 P(X ≥ 9) = (220 + 66 + 12 + 1)/4096; A1 = 0.0730; A1 0.0730 > 0.05, do not reject H₀.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A brick kiln near Gujranwala claims that the median compressive strength of its bricks is 300 units. A buyer tests 14 bricks:
312, 287, 345, 298, 276, 305, 291, 283, 268, 299, 277, 302, 289, 294
Use a sign test at the 5% significance level to test whether the median strength is less than 300.
parts.answer: 4 above, 10 below; P(X ≤ 4) = 0.0898; do not reject H₀
parts.working: B1 H₀: median = 300, H₁: median < 300; M1 count signs: 4 '+', 10 '−'; M1 X ~ B(14, 0.5); M1 P(X ≤ 4); A1 0.0898; A1 do not reject H₀; insufficient evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sample of 16 commuters in Mumbai each record their journey times on a weekday by bus and by metro. In 3 cases the bus is faster, in 12 cases the metro is faster and in 1 case the times are equal. Use a sign test at the 5% significance level to test whether there is a difference between median journey times by bus and by metro.
parts.answer: P(X ≤ 3) = 0.0176; reject H₀: evidence of a difference
parts.working: B1 H₀: median difference = 0, H₁: ≠ 0; B1 discard the tie: n = 15; M1 X ~ B(15, 0.5), X = 3; M1 P(X ≤ 3) = (1 + 15 + 105 + 455)/32768; A1 0.0176; A1 compare with 0.025 (two-tailed): reject H₀; evidence of a difference in median times.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a survey of 44 randomly chosen shoppers at a market in Cairo, each rates two brands of dates on a 10-point scale. 27 rate brand A higher, 13 rate brand B higher and 4 give equal ratings. Use a sign test with a suitable normal approximation, at the 5% significance level, to test whether brand A is preferred.
parts.answer: z = 2.055; reject H₀: evidence that brand A is preferred
parts.working: B1 H₀: p = 0.5, H₁: p > 0.5; B1 n = 40 after removing ties; M1 X ~ B(40, 0.5) ≈ N(20, 10); M1 z = (26.5 − 20)/√10 with continuity correction; A1 z = 2.055; A1 2.055 > 1.645: reject H₀, evidence that brand A is preferred.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Eleven athletes in Addis Ababa have their resting heart rate (beats per minute) measured before and after an 8-week training camp.
Before: 68, 74, 81, 59, 77, 70, 85, 66, 72, 79, 63
After: 65, 74, 76, 61, 70, 66, 80, 66, 69, 74, 58
Use a sign test at the 1% significance level to test whether training lowers the median resting heart rate.
parts.answer: 8 decreases, 1 increase, 2 unchanged; P(X ≥ 8) = 0.0195; do not reject H₀: insufficient evidence at the 1% level
parts.working: B1 H₀: median (before − after) = 0, H₁: > 0; M1 signs of differences, ignoring 2 zeros: n = 9; M1 X ~ B(9, 0.5), X = 8; M1 P(X ≥ 8); A1 0.0195; A1 do not reject H₀ at 1%; insufficient evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sign test is to be used with 20 non-zero differences to test H₀: median difference = 0 against H₁: median difference > 0, at the 5% significance level. X is the number of positive differences. Find the critical region and the actual significance level of the test.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In fact 70% of differences in the population are positive. Find the probability that the test leads to rejection of H₀.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A taxi company in Doha believes the median waiting time for a taxi at a mall is more than 5.8 minutes. A random sample of 10 waiting times (minutes) is:
4.6, 5.9, 6.3, 5.2, 7.4, 6.8, 5.5, 8.1, 6.1, 7.0
Carry out a sign test at the 5% significance level.
parts.answer: 7 above, 3 below; P(X ≥ 7) = 0.172; do not reject H₀
parts.working: B1 H₀: median = 5.8, H₁: median > 5.8; M1 X ~ B(10, 0.5), X = 7; M1 P(X ≥ 7); A1 0.172; A1 do not reject H₀; insufficient evidence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Carry out a Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the same data at the 5% significance level, and comment on the two conclusions.
parts.answer: T = 15; critical value 10; do not reject H₀; both tests agree
parts.working: M1 ranks: 0.1→1, −0.3→2.5, 0.3→2.5, 0.5→4, −0.6→5, 1→6, −1.2→7.5, 1.2→7.5, 1.6→9, 2.3→10; A1 P = 40, Q = 15, T = 15; B1 critical value 10; A1 do not reject H₀; B1 comment: Wilcoxon uses magnitudes as well as signs (more powerful) but needs a symmetric distribution.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The times (minutes) taken to assemble a flat-pack desk are recorded for 5 people using printed instructions (A) and 6 people using a video guide (B).
A: 23.4, 27.1, 21.8, 25.6, 22.9
B: 28.3, 26.4, 30.2, 24.7, 29.5, 31.0
Use a Wilcoxon rank-sum test at the 5% significance level to test whether people using printed instructions tend to be quicker.
parts.answer: R_A = 18; W = 18; critical value 20; reject H₀: evidence that printed instructions are quicker
parts.working: B1 H₀: the two populations have equal medians, H₁: median time for A is less; M1 rank all 11 times; M1 sum of ranks of the smaller sample A: R_A = 18; A1 m(m + n + 1) − R_A = 60 − 18 = 42, W = 18; B1 critical value (m = 5, n = 6, 5% one-tailed) 20; M1 compare; A1 reject H₀; evidence that printed instructions lead to quicker assembly.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A biologist counts the number of earthworms in randomly chosen 1 m² plots in two orchards near Swat.
Orchard A (6 plots): 14, 19, 11, 17, 22, 16
Orchard B (8 plots): 21, 25, 18, 24, 19, 27, 23, 26
Test at the 5% significance level whether there is a difference between the median numbers of earthworms per plot in the two orchards. Give tied values the mean of their ranks.
parts.answer: R_A = 25.5; W = 25.5; critical value 29; reject H₀: evidence of a difference
parts.working: B1 H₀: no difference in population medians, H₁: medians differ; M1 rank all 14 with ties averaged: 11(A)→1, 14(A)→2, 16(A)→3, 17(A)→4, 18(B)→5, 19(A)→6.5, 21(B)→8, 22(A)→9, 23(B)→10, 24(B)→11, 25(B)→12, 26(B)→13, 27(B)→14; A1 R_A = 25.5; M1 W = min(25.5, 90 − 25.5) = 25.5; B1 two-tailed 5% critical value for m = 6, n = 8: 29; A1 reject H₀; evidence that the median numbers differ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The ages of 12 randomly chosen customers at a café in Istanbul and 15 at a café in Ankara are ranked together, from youngest (rank 1). The sum of the ranks of the Istanbul customers is 131. Using a normal approximation, test at the 5% significance level whether there is a difference between the median ages of customers at the two cafés.
parts.answer: W = 131; z = −1.781; do not reject H₀
parts.working: B1 H₀: equal population medians, H₁: different; M1 m(m + n + 1) − R = 336 − 131 = 205, W = 131; B1 mean 168, variance 12 × 15 × 28/12 = 420; M1 z = (131 + 0.5 − 168)/√420; A1 z = −1.781; M1 compare with −1.96; A1 do not reject H₀.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Fourteen students in Singapore are split at random into two groups of 7. Group A learns vocabulary using flash cards, group B using a mobile app. Their test scores are:
A: 52, 61, 48, 57, 66, 55, 59
B: 63, 58, 70, 67, 72, 64, 69
Use a Wilcoxon rank-sum test at the 5% significance level to test whether there is a difference in median scores.
parts.answer: R_A = 33; W = 33; critical value 36; reject H₀: evidence of a difference
parts.working: B1 H₀: equal population medians, H₁: medians differ; M1 rank the combined scores: 48(A)→1, 52(A)→2, 55(A)→3, 57(A)→4, 58(B)→5, 59(A)→6, 61(A)→7, 63(B)→8, 64(B)→9, 66(A)→10, 67(B)→11, 69(B)→12, 70(B)→13, 72(B)→14; A1 R_A = 33; M1 7 × 15 − 33 = 72, W = 33; B1 critical value 36; A1 reject H₀; evidence that median scores differ (the app group scores higher).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why a rank-sum test might be chosen here instead of a two-sample t-test.
parts.answer: The scores may not be normally distributed (small samples; distribution unknown)
parts.working: B1 no assumption of normality needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A chemist in Riyadh compares the yield (g) of a reaction with a new catalyst (B, 7 trials) and the old catalyst (A, 4 trials).
A: 8.2, 9.7, 7.5, 8.9
B: 10.4, 9.1, 11.8, 10.9, 9.9, 12.3, 10.1
Test at the 1% significance level whether the new catalyst gives a higher median yield.
parts.answer: R_A = 11; W = 11; critical value 11; reject H₀: evidence that the new catalyst gives higher yields
parts.working: B1 H₀: equal medians, H₁: median for B is greater; M1 ranks: 7.5(A)→1, 8.2(A)→2, 8.9(A)→3, 9.1(B)→4, 9.7(A)→5, 9.9(B)→6, 10.1(B)→7, 10.4(B)→8, 10.9(B)→9, 11.8(B)→10, 12.3(B)→11; A1 R_A = 11; A1 W = 11; B1 critical value (m = 4, n = 7, 1% one-tailed) 11; A1 reject H₀; strong evidence that the new catalyst increases the median yield.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the smallest possible value of R_A. Given that the critical value for a 0.5% one-tailed test with these sample sizes is 10, state what the data would have to look like for H₀ to be rejected at that level.
parts.answer: Smallest R_A = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10; need W = 10, i.e. all four old-catalyst yields lower than every new-catalyst yield
parts.working: B1 10; B1 W ≤ 10 only when R_A = 10, so the four A values must take ranks 1 to 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A Wilcoxon rank-sum test is to compare a sample of 20 tomato plants grown with compost and 25 grown without, using the heights after 8 weeks. The test is one-tailed at the 5% level, H₁ being that compost-grown plants tend to be taller. The plants are ranked from tallest (rank 1). Give the mean and variance of the rank sum R of the compost sample under H₀.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using a normal approximation with continuity correction, find the largest value of R that leads to H₀ being rejected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The compost plants have R = 382. State the conclusion.
parts.answer: Reject H₀: evidence that compost-grown plants tend to be taller

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher measures the cholesterol level of 9 patients before and after a change of diet. She considers a sign test, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test and a paired-sample t-test. State the assumption about the population of differences needed for (i) the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and (ii) the paired-sample t-test.
parts.answer: (i) the differences have a symmetric distribution; (ii) the differences are normally distributed
parts.working: B1 symmetric; B1 normal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Wilcoxon signed-rank test is generally preferred to the sign test when its assumption holds.
parts.answer: It uses the magnitudes of the differences as well as their signs, so it uses more information and is more powerful
parts.working: B1 uses sizes (ranks) of differences, not just signs; B1 more powerful / more likely to detect a real difference.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each situation, name the most suitable non-parametric test and give a reason.
(i) The weights of 8 randomly chosen goats from one farm and 10 from another farm are compared; nothing is known about the distribution of weights.
(ii) 25 people each rate two films as 'better' or 'worse' than the other, and only the preferences are recorded.
(iii) The times of 12 runners on two different tracks are compared; the differences can be assumed to have a symmetric distribution.
parts.answer: (i) Wilcoxon rank-sum test: two independent samples; (ii) sign test: only the direction of each preference is known; (iii) Wilcoxon signed-rank test: paired data with symmetric differences
parts.working: B1 each test with a valid reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In (iii), a student instead uses a sign test. Explain why this is valid but less appropriate.
parts.answer: The sign test needs no symmetry assumption so is valid, but it ignores the sizes of the differences and is less powerful
parts.working: B1 valid but wastes information.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The differences (new method − old method) in the yield of a reaction for 10 paired trials are:
3.1, −0.4, 2.6, 1.8, −0.7, 4.2, 2.2, 0.9, 3.5, −0.2
Carry out a one-tailed sign test and a one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test, each at the 5% significance level, to test whether the new method increases the median yield.
parts.answer: Sign test: P(X ≥ 7) = 0.172, do not reject H₀; Wilcoxon: T = 6, critical value 10, reject H₀

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the two tests can reach different conclusions, and state which you would rely on, with a reason.
parts.answer: The negative differences are all small, which the Wilcoxon test takes into account but the sign test ignores; rely on the Wilcoxon test if the differences are symmetric, otherwise the sign test
parts.working: B1 Wilcoxon uses magnitudes (small negative ranks); B1 choice with the symmetry condition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express 1 + i√3 in the form r e^(iθ), where r > 0 and −π < θ ≤ π.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence use de Moivre's theorem to find (1 + i√3)⁸ in the form a + ib, where a and b are exact.

parts.label: a

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use de Moivre's theorem to show that sin 3θ = 3sin θ − 4sin³θ.
parts.working: M1 (cos θ + i sin θ)³ = cos 3θ + i sin 3θ; M1 expand, imaginary part 3cos²θ sin θ − sin³θ; M1 cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ; A1 3sin θ − 4sin³θ (AG).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of ∫ sin³θ dθ with limits 0 and ½π.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By writing z = cos θ + i sin θ and using z + 1/z = 2cos θ, show that cos⁴θ = ⅛(cos 4θ + 4cos 2θ + 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of ∫ cos⁴θ dθ with limits 0 and ¼π.
parts.working: M1 [⅛(¼sin 4θ + 2sin 2θ + 3θ)]; M1 limits; A1 ⅛(2 + 3π/4) = ¼ + 3π/32.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use de Moivre's theorem to show that cos 5θ = 16cos⁵θ − 20cos³θ + 5cos θ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of 16cos⁵(π/10) − 20cos³(π/10) + 5cos(π/10).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use de Moivre's theorem to show that tan 3θ = (3t − t³)/(1 − 3t²), where t = tan θ.
parts.working: M1 cos 3θ = c³ − 3cs², sin 3θ = 3c²s − s³; M1 divide; M1 by c³; A1 (AG).

parts.label: b
parts.text: By considering tan 3θ = 1, show that t = tan(π/12) is a root of t³ − 3t² − 3t + 1 = 0.
parts.working: M1 3t − t³ = 1 − 3t²; A1 rearranged, and tan(3 × π/12) = 1 (AG).

parts.label: c

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using z = cos θ + i sin θ and z − 1/z = 2i sin θ, show that sin⁵θ = (1/16)(sin 5θ − 5sin 3θ + 10sin θ).
parts.working: M1 (z − 1/z)⁵ = 32i sin⁵θ; M1 expand: (z⁵ − z⁻⁵) − 5(z³ − z⁻³) + 10(z − z⁻¹); M1 zⁿ − z⁻ⁿ = 2i sin nθ; A1 32i sin⁵θ = 2i(sin 5θ − 5sin 3θ + 10sin θ); A1 (AG).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of ∫ sin⁵θ dθ with limits 0 and ½π.
parts.working: M1 integrate each term; M1 values 1/5, 1/3, 1; A1 (1/16)(1/5 − 5/3 + 10) = 8/15.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the smallest positive integer n for which (√3 + i)ⁿ is a negative real number, and state the value of (√3 + i)ⁿ for this n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use de Moivre's theorem to show that sin 6θ / sin θ = 32cos⁵θ − 32cos³θ + 6cos θ, for sin θ ≠ 0.
parts.working: M1 Im(c + is)⁶ = 6c⁵s − 20c³s³ + 6cs⁵; M1 divide by s; M1 s² = 1 − c², s⁴ = (1 − c²)²; M1 expand; A1 collect: 6c⁵ − 20c³ + 20c⁵ + 6c − 12c³ + 6c⁵; A1 32c⁵ − 32c³ + 6c (AG).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the values of cos θ, for 0 < θ < π, which satisfy sin 6θ = 6cos θ sin θ, giving exact answers.
parts.working: M1 32c⁵ − 32c³ = 0; M1 c = 0 or c² = 1; A1 c = ±1 gives sin θ = 0, not in range, so cos θ = 0 (θ = ½π).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that cos⁵θ = (1/16)(cos 5θ + 5cos 3θ + 10cos θ).
parts.working: M1 (z + 1/z)⁵ = 32cos⁵θ; M1 expand binomially; M1 pair terms as 2cos nθ; A1 (AG).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of ∫ cos⁵θ dθ with limits 0 and ⅓π.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use de Moivre's theorem to show that cos 4θ = 8cos⁴θ − 8cos²θ + 1.
parts.working: M1 Re(c + is)⁴ = c⁴ − 6c²s² + s⁴; M1 s² = 1 − c²; A1 c⁴ − 6c² + 6c⁴ + 1 − 2c² + c⁴; A1 (AG).

parts.label: b
parts.text: By considering the equation cos 4θ = 0, show that cos(π/8) = ½√(2 + √2).
parts.working: M1 8c⁴ − 8c² + 1 = 0 with roots cos(π/8), cos(3π/8), …; M1 c² = (2 ± √2)/4; A1 cos(π/8) is the largest positive root so take +; A1 c = ½√(2 + √2) (AG).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that 1 + cos 2θ + i sin 2θ = 2cos θ (cos θ + i sin θ).
parts.working: M1 1 + cos 2θ = 2cos²θ, sin 2θ = 2sin θ cos θ; A1 factorise (AG).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence show that (1 + cos 2θ + i sin 2θ)ⁿ = 2ⁿcosⁿθ (cos nθ + i sin nθ), and find the exact real part of (1 + cos 2θ + i sin 2θ)⁴ when θ = π/6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use de Moivre's theorem to show that sin²θ cos⁴θ = (1/32)(2 + cos 2θ − 2cos 4θ − cos 6θ).
parts.working: M1 (z + 1/z)⁴(z − 1/z)² = (2cos θ)⁴(2i sin θ)² = −64 sin²θ cos⁴θ; M1 (z + 1/z)²(z² − 1/z²)²; M1 expand: z⁶ + z⁻⁶ + 2(z⁴ + z⁻⁴) − (z² + z⁻²) − 4; M1 = 2cos 6θ + 4cos 4θ − 2cos 2θ − 4; A1 divide by −64; A1 (AG).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of ∫ sin²θ cos⁴θ dθ with limits 0 and ½π.
parts.working: M1 the cosine terms integrate to 0 over [0, ½π]; A1 (1/32)(2 × ½π) = π/32.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that cos 3θ = 4cos³θ − 3cos θ, show that the substitution x = cos θ turns the equation 8x³ − 6x − 1 = 0 into cos 3θ = ½.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that cos 5θ = 16cos⁵θ − 20cos³θ + 5cos θ, show that the non-zero roots of 16x⁴ − 20x² + 5 = 0 are cos(π/10), cos(3π/10), cos(7π/10) and cos(9π/10).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use de Moivre's theorem to show that sin 5θ = 16sin⁵θ − 20sin³θ + 5sin θ.
parts.working: M1 Im(c + is)⁵ = 5c⁴s − 10c²s³ + s⁵; M1 c² = 1 − s²; A1 expand; A1 (AG).

parts.working: M1 sin 5θ = 0, θ = π/5, 2π/5 give non-zero s with 16s⁴ − 20s² + 5 = 0; A1 y = s²; M1 y = (5 ± √5)/8; A1 sin²(π/5) < sin²(2π/5), so (5 − √5)/8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation z⁵ = 1, giving the roots in the form e^(iθ), where −π < θ ≤ π.

A1: e^(5(t−1)) is the PGF of Po(5); mean 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(X + Y ≤ 1) in the form ke⁻⁵, and give its value correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.text: A random variable X has PGF G(t) = (1 + 2t + t²)/4. Three independent observations X₁, X₂, X₃ are taken and S = X₁ + X₂ + X₃. Show that the PGF of S can be written as ((1 + t)/2)⁶.

parts.label: b

parts.label: b

parts.label: a
parts.text: A game uses a fair three-sided spinner labelled 0, 1, 2. The spinner is spun three times and S is the total score. Find the PGF of S and hence find P(S = 3).
parts.working:
B1: single spin G(t) = (1 + t + t²)/3.
M1: G_S = G(t)³.
M1: (1 + t + t²)³ = 1 + 3t + 6t² + 7t³ + 6t⁴ + 3t⁵ + t⁶.

practice.subtopic: PGF of a sum of independent variables

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cricketer in a practice session hits a six on any ball with probability 1/4, independently. X₁ is the number of balls up to and including her first six, and X₂ is the number of further balls up to and including her second six. Write down the PGF of X₁ and find the PGF of N = X₁ + X₂.
parts.working:
B1: geometric PGF t/(4 − 3t).
M1: X₁, X₂ independent, identically distributed: square.
A1: G_N = t²/(4 − 3t)².

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

parts.working:
B1: binomial factor.
B1: Poisson factor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Each of n independent identical components in a solar panel array either works (scored 1) or fails (scored 0); the score of one component has PGF (1 + 2t)/3. S_n is the total score of the n components. Write down the PGF of S_n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the least n for which P(S_n = 0) < 0.01.

parts.label: c

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The number of power cuts, X, in a town on a summer day has the distribution
x: 0, 1, 2, 3
P(X = x): 0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05.
Write down the probability generating function of X.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use G(t) to find E(X) and Var(X).

parts.label: a
parts.text: X ~ B(n, p). Show that the probability generating function of X is (q + pt)ⁿ, where q = 1 − p.
parts.working:
M1: G(t) = Σ ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ tʳ = Σ ⁿCᵣ (pt)ʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ.
A1: = (q + pt)ⁿ by the binomial theorem.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A quiz in an Urdu class has 5 multiple-choice questions, each guessed correctly with probability 0.2 independently. Use the PGF of the number of correct guesses to find its mean and variance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal takes his driving test repeatedly until he passes. The probability that he passes on any attempt is 0.35, independently. X is the number of attempts needed. Show that the PGF of X is G(t) = 0.35t/(1 − 0.65t), stating the range of t for which it is valid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use G(t) to find E(X) and Var(X), correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: X ~ Po(λ). Show that the PGF of X is e^(λ(t − 1)).
parts.working:
M1: G(t) = Σ e^(−λ) λʳ tʳ/r! = e^(−λ) Σ (λt)ʳ/r!.
A1: = e^(−λ) e^(λt) = e^(λ(t−1)).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence show that E(X) = Var(X) = λ.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The number of calls to a helpline per minute is Po(1.5). By considering G(1) + G(−1), find the probability that the number of calls in a given minute is even, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A random variable X has P(X = r) = k/2ʳ for r = 1, 2, 3, 4, and zero otherwise. Find k and write down the PGF of X.

parts.label: b

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bag contains 3 red and 2 blue marbles. Marbles are taken out one at a time, at random and without replacement, until a red marble is obtained. X is the number of marbles taken out. Find the probability distribution of X and write down its PGF.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use G(t) to find E(X) and Var(X).

parts.text: A random variable X has PGF G(t) = ((2 + t)/3)ⁿ, where n is a positive integer. Given that E(X) = 2, find n.

parts.label: b

parts.text: A random variable X takes values 0, 1, 2, … with P(X = r) = (r + 1)/2^(r+2). Show that the PGF of X is G(t) = 1/(2 − t)².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find E(X) and Var(X).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find P(X ≤ 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a board game, a player must throw a six with a fair dice to start. Y is the number of throws needed. Show that the PGF of Y is G(t) = t/(6 − 5t).

parts.label: b

parts.label: c
parts.text: Two players, Ayesha and Daniyal, take turns to throw the dice, Ayesha first; the first to throw a six starts the game. Use part (b) to state the probability that Ayesha starts.
parts.working: B1: Ayesha starts exactly when the total number of throws is odd.
