parts.label: a
parts.text:
A board-game club in Rawalpindi suspects that one of its dice is biased. The die is thrown 120 times with these results.
Score: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Frequency: 15, 25, 18, 22, 16, 24
Test, at the 5% significance level, whether the die is fair.
parts.answer: X² = 4.50, ν = 5, critical value 11.07; 4.50 < 11.07, so do not reject H₀: there is insufficient evidence that the die is biased
parts.working: B1 H₀: the die is fair (each score has probability 1/6); H₁: the die is not fair; M1 each expected frequency 120/6 = 20; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 4.50; B1 ν = 5, critical value 11.07; A1 4.50 < 11.07, so do not reject H₀: there is insufficient evidence that the die is biased.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A plant breeder crosses two varieties of pea. Genetic theory predicts the four types of offspring (round-yellow, round-green, wrinkled-yellow, wrinkled-green) in the ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. In a sample of 160 offspring the observed frequencies were 95, 28, 30 and 7 respectively. Calculate the expected frequencies.
parts.working: M1 160 × 9/16 etc.; A1 all four correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Test, at the 5% significance level, whether the data are consistent with the theory.
parts.answer: X² = 1.31, ν = 3, critical value 7.815; 1.31 < 7.815, so do not reject H₀: the data are consistent with the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio
parts.working: B1 H₀: the ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 is a good model; H₁: it is not; M1 use of expected values from (a); M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 1.31; B1 ν = 3, critical value 7.815; A1 1.31 < 7.815, so do not reject H₀: the data are consistent with the ratio.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The head teacher of a school in Lahore records the number of student absences on each weekday over one term.
Day: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday
Absences: 50, 28, 26, 30, 46
Test, at the 5% significance level, whether absences are equally likely to occur on each weekday.
parts.answer: X² = 13.8, ν = 4, critical value 9.488; 13.8 > 9.488, so reject H₀: absences are not equally likely on each weekday
parts.working: B1 H₀: absences are uniformly distributed over the five days; H₁: they are not; M1 each expected frequency 180/5 = 36; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 13.8; B1 ν = 4, critical value 9.488; A1 13.8 > 9.488, so reject H₀: absences are not equally likely on each weekday.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which days contribute most to the value of the test statistic and suggest a reason in context.
parts.answer: Monday and Friday (O − E = 14 and 10, contributions 5.44 and 2.78); students may be extending their weekends
parts.working: B1 Monday and Friday identified with contributions; B1 sensible reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A commuter in Karachi notes the number of minutes past the hour at which 120 buses arrived at a stop. The times are grouped into ten-minute intervals.
Minutes past the hour: 0–, 10–, 20–, 30–, 40–, 50–60
Frequency: 28, 16, 18, 22, 14, 22
Test, at the 10% significance level, whether the arrival time (in minutes past the hour) can be modelled by a continuous uniform distribution on [0, 60].
parts.answer: X² = 6.40, ν = 5, critical value 9.236; 6.40 < 9.236, so do not reject H₀: the uniform distribution is a suitable model
parts.working: B1 H₀: arrival time ~ U(0, 60); H₁: it does not follow this distribution; M1 each interval has probability 1/6, expected frequency 20; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 6.40; B1 ν = 5, critical value 9.236; A1 6.40 < 9.236, so do not reject H₀: the uniform model is suitable.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A proof-reader claims that the number of typing errors per page in a long report has distribution Po(0.8). She checks 100 pages.
Errors: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or more
Pages: 40, 38, 15, 5, 2
The expected frequencies are 44.93, 35.95, 14.38, 3.83 and 0.91. Explain why some classes must be combined, and state the classes you will use.
parts.answer: Expected frequencies below 5 make the χ² approximation unreliable; 3.83 + 0.91 = 4.74 is still below 5, so use classes 0, 1 and '2 or more'
parts.working: B1 reason; B1 correct classes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Test the claim at the 5% significance level.
parts.answer: X² = 1.09, ν = 2, critical value 5.991; 1.09 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: Po(0.8) is a suitable model
parts.working: B1 H₀: Po(0.8) is a good model; H₁: it is not; M1 O = 40, 38, 22 and E = 44.93, 35.95, 19.12; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 1.09; B1 ν = 2 (3 − 1), critical value 5.991; A1 1.09 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: Po(0.8) suitable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A health survey claims that the proportions of people with blood groups O, A, B and AB in a region are 0.35, 0.23, 0.33 and 0.09. A blood bank records the groups of 300 donors: 96, 75, 105 and 24 respectively. Test, at the 5% significance level, whether the donors are consistent with the claimed proportions.
parts.answer: X² = 1.99, ν = 3, critical value 7.815; 1.99 < 7.815, so do not reject H₀: the donors are consistent with the claimed proportions
parts.working: B1 H₀: the claimed proportions are correct for donors; H₁: they are not; M1 expected 105, 69, 99, 27; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 1.99; B1 ν = 3, critical value 7.815; A1 1.99 < 7.815, so do not reject H₀: consistent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A spinner has sectors labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4. Its designer says that the score X satisfies P(X = x) = x/10 for x = 1, 2, 3, 4. In 200 spins the scores 1, 2, 3, 4 occurred 24, 38, 62 and 76 times. Test, at the 5% significance level, whether the designer's model fits the data.
parts.answer: X² = 1.17, ν = 3, critical value 7.815; 1.17 < 7.815, so do not reject H₀: the model fits the data
parts.working: B1 H₀: P(X = x) = x/10 is a good model; H₁: it is not; M1 expected 20, 40, 60, 80; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 1.17; B1 ν = 3, critical value 7.815; A1 1.17 < 7.815, so do not reject H₀: the model fits.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A factory in Sialkot packs footballs in boxes of 4. The manager claims that each ball independently has probability 0.2 of having a minor defect. One hundred boxes are inspected and the number of defective balls in each box is recorded.
Number defective: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
Number of boxes: 38, 42, 15, 4, 1
Calculate the expected frequencies under the manager's claim.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Carry out a goodness-of-fit test at the 5% significance level, explaining any combining of classes.
parts.answer: X² = 0.444, ν = 2, critical value 5.991; 0.444 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: B(4, 0.2) is a suitable model
parts.working: B1 H₀: B(4, 0.2) is a good model; H₁: it is not; M1 combine 2, 3 and 4 since expected frequencies 2.56 and 0.16 are less than 5: O = 20, E = 18.08; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 0.444; B1 ν = 2 (3 classes − 1; p was given), critical value 5.991; A1 0.444 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: B(4, 0.2) is a suitable model.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A survey records the number of girls in 200 families that each have exactly three children.
Number of girls: 0, 1, 2, 3
Number of families: 22, 70, 78, 30
Show that the estimate of p, the probability that a child is a girl, is 0.527 to 3 significant figures, and calculate the expected frequencies for a binomial model with this p.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Test, at the 5% significance level, whether a binomial distribution is a suitable model.
parts.answer: X² = 0.0671, ν = 2, critical value 5.991; 0.0671 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: a binomial distribution is a suitable model
parts.working: B1 H₀: B(3, p) is a good model; H₁: it is not; M1 expected frequencies from (a), all at least 5; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 0.0671; B1 ν = 2 (4 − 1 − 1, since p was estimated), critical value 5.991; A1 0.0671 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: binomial is a suitable model.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The number of calls arriving per minute at a telephone help desk in Karachi was recorded for 150 one-minute periods.
Number of calls: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or more
Frequency: 30, 48, 30, 18, 12, 12
The supervisor believes the number of calls per minute follows the distribution Po(2). Calculate the expected frequencies.
parts.working: M1 150 × e⁻²2ᵏ/k!; A1 first five correct; A1 last by subtraction 7.90.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Test the supervisor's belief at the 5% significance level.
parts.answer: X² = 14.1, ν = 5, critical value 11.07; 14.1 > 11.07, so reject H₀: Po(2) is not a good model
parts.working: B1 H₀: Po(2) is a good model; H₁: it is not; M1 all expected frequencies exceed 5, so no combining; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 14.1; B1 ν = 5 (6 − 1, λ given), critical value 11.07; A1 14.1 > 11.07, so reject H₀: Po(2) is not a good model.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A driving school records how many attempts each of 150 learners needed to pass the driving test.
Attempts: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or more
Learners: 76, 28, 14, 10, 22
The instructor suggests the number of attempts follows a geometric distribution Geo(0.4). Calculate the expected frequencies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Test at the 5% significance level whether Geo(0.4) is a suitable model.
parts.answer: X² = 9.73, ν = 4, critical value 9.488; 9.73 > 9.488, so reject H₀: Geo(0.4) is not a suitable model
parts.working: B1 H₀: Geo(0.4) is a good model; H₁: it is not; M1 expected frequencies from (a); M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 9.73; B1 ν = 4 (5 − 1), critical value 9.488; A1 9.73 > 9.488, so reject H₀: Geo(0.4) not suitable.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The heights, h cm, of 200 seedlings in a nursery near Murree are summarised below.
Height: h < 20, 20 ≤ h < 25, 25 ≤ h < 30, 30 ≤ h < 35, 35 ≤ h < 40, h ≥ 40
Frequency: 6, 30, 66, 62, 28, 8
It is suggested that heights are distributed N(30, 5²). Calculate the expected frequencies for each class.
parts.working: M1 standardise boundaries to z = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2; M1 200 × probabilities; A1 4.55, 27.18, 68.27, 68.27, 27.18, 4.55.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Test at the 5% significance level whether the suggested distribution is a good fit.
parts.answer: X² = 1.80, ν = 3, critical value 7.815; 1.80 < 7.815, so do not reject H₀: N(30, 5²) is a good fit
parts.working: B1 H₀: N(30, 5²) is a good model; H₁: it is not; M1 combine end classes with neighbours (4.55 < 5): O = 36, 66, 62, 36; E = 31.73, 68.27, 68.27, 31.73; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 1.80; B1 ν = 3 (4 − 1, parameters given), critical value 7.815; A1 1.80 < 7.815, so do not reject H₀: a good fit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A random variable X, the proportion of a daily water tank in a Quetta household that is used by noon, is thought to have probability density function f(x) = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. Show that P(0.25 ≤ X < 0.5) = 3/16.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
On 100 days the observed values were grouped as follows.
x: 0–0.25, 0.25–0.5, 0.5–0.75, 0.75–1
Frequency: 3, 12, 27, 58
Test at the 5% significance level whether f is a suitable model.
parts.answer: X² = 9.34, ν = 3, critical value 7.815; 9.34 > 7.815, so reject H₀: f is not a suitable model
parts.working: B1 H₀: f(x) = 2x is a good model; H₁: it is not; M1 probabilities 1/16, 3/16, 5/16, 7/16; M1 expected 6.25, 18.75, 31.25, 43.75; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 9.34; B1 ν = 3, critical value 7.815; A1 9.34 > 7.815, so reject H₀: f not suitable.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A biologist models the number of eggs laid by a species of bird in a nest. The model has two parameters, both estimated from the data. For 120 nests:
Eggs: 1, 2, 3, 4 or more
Observed: 12, 30, 41, 37
Expected (from the fitted model): 15, 28, 40, 37
State the number of degrees of freedom for a goodness-of-fit test, justifying your answer.
parts.working: M1 one degree of freedom lost because the totals agree and one for each estimated parameter; A1 ν = 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Carry out the test at the 5% significance level.
parts.answer: X² = 0.768, ν = 1, critical value 3.841; 0.768 < 3.841, so do not reject H₀: the model is suitable
parts.working: M1 X² = 9/15 + 4/28 + 1/40 + 0 = 0.768; B1 critical value 3.841; M1 compare; A1 0.768 < 3.841, so do not reject H₀: the model is suitable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A toy company asked 60 children in Islamabad to choose their favourite of four colours for a new toy: red, blue, green and yellow. The choices were 20, 14, 10 and 16 respectively. Test, at the 5% significance level, whether all four colours are equally popular.
parts.answer: X² = 3.47, ν = 3, critical value 7.815; 3.47 < 7.815, so do not reject H₀: there is insufficient evidence that the colours differ in popularity
parts.working: B1 H₀: the four colours are equally popular; H₁: they are not; M1 each expected frequency 15; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 3.47; B1 ν = 3, critical value 7.815; A1 3.47 < 7.815, so do not reject H₀: insufficient evidence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A larger survey of 180 children produced exactly the same proportions choosing each colour. Show that the test statistic is now three times as large and state the conclusion of the same test.
parts.answer: X² = 10.4 (= 3 × 3.47); 10.4 > 7.815, reject H₀: the colours are not equally popular
parts.working: M1 every O and E is multiplied by 3, so each (O − E)²/E is multiplied by 9/3 = 3; A1 X² = 10.4; A1 exceeds 7.815, conclusion reverses.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on what this shows about the effect of sample size on a goodness-of-fit test.
parts.answer: Larger samples make the test more sensitive (more powerful): the same proportional discrepancy becomes significant
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The numbers of goals scored by a hockey team in 80 league matches are shown.
Goals: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Matches: 20, 28, 18, 9, 4, 1
Calculate the mean number of goals per match.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fit a Poisson distribution with this mean, treating the last class as '3 or more' after any necessary combining, and test at the 10% significance level whether the Poisson distribution is a suitable model.
parts.answer: X² = 0.136, ν = 2, critical value 4.605; 0.136 < 4.605, so do not reject H₀: a Poisson distribution is a suitable model
parts.working: B1 H₀: a Poisson distribution is a good model; H₁: it is not; M1 expected frequencies 19.73, 27.62, 19.33, 9.02, 3.16, 1.14 (last as ≥ 5); M1 combine to '3 or more': O = 14, E = 13.32; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 0.136; B1 ν = 2 (4 − 1 − 1, mean estimated), critical value 4.605; A1 0.136 < 4.605, so do not reject H₀: Poisson is a suitable model.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give a reason, in context, why a Poisson model might be expected here.
parts.answer: Goals occur singly, at random and independently, at a roughly constant average rate during matches
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The masses, m grams, of 150 mangoes from an orchard near Multan are grouped as follows.
Mass: m < 220, 220 ≤ m < 240, 240 ≤ m < 260, 260 ≤ m < 280, m ≥ 280
Frequency: 12, 38, 58, 30, 12
From the raw data, the sample mean is 250 g and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation is 20 g. Fit a normal distribution with these parameters and calculate the expected frequencies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Test at the 5% significance level whether a normal distribution is a suitable model for the masses.
parts.answer: X² = 1.95, ν = 2, critical value 5.991; 1.95 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: a normal distribution is a suitable model
parts.working: B1 H₀: a normal distribution is a good model; H₁: it is not; M1 expected frequencies from (a), all at least 5; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 1.95; B1 ν = 2 (5 − 1 − 2, since μ and σ were estimated), critical value 5.991; A1 1.95 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: normal is suitable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the number of degrees of freedom would be different if the mean and standard deviation had been given rather than estimated.
parts.answer: Each estimated parameter is a restriction that removes one degree of freedom; with given parameters ν = 4
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The lifetimes, T years, of 200 solar-panel inverters are recorded.
T: 0 ≤ T < 1, 1 ≤ T < 2, 2 ≤ T < 4, T ≥ 4
Frequency: 62, 58, 56, 24
A manufacturer claims that T has probability density function f(t) = 0.5e^(−0.5t) for t ≥ 0. Find the cumulative distribution function F(t) and hence calculate the expected frequencies under this claim.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Test the manufacturer's claim at the 5% significance level.
parts.answer: X² = 8.04, ν = 3, critical value 7.815; 8.04 > 7.815, so reject H₀: the claimed distribution is not a good model
parts.working: B1 H₀: f(t) = 0.5e^(−0.5t) is a good model; H₁: it is not; M1 expected frequencies from (a); M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 8.04; B1 ν = 3 (4 − 1), critical value 7.815; A1 8.04 > 7.815, so reject H₀: claim not supported.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A quality inspector tests packets of 5 seeds and records how many seeds in each of 150 packets fail to germinate.
Failures: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Packets: 30, 52, 40, 20, 6, 2
Estimate p, the probability that a seed fails to germinate, correct to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected frequencies for a binomial model with this p and carry out a goodness-of-fit test at the 5% significance level.
parts.answer: X² = 2.41, ν = 2, critical value 5.991; 2.41 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: the binomial model is suitable
parts.working: B1 H₀: B(5, p) is a good model; H₁: it is not; M1 expected 24.97, 53.85, 46.45, 20.03, 4.32, 0.37; M1 combine 3, 4, 5 (E for 4 and 5 together is 4.69 < 5): O = 28, E = 24.73; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 2.41; B1 ν = 2 (4 − 1 − 1, p estimated), critical value 5.991; A1 2.41 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: binomial suitable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a reason, in context, why the binomial model might not be appropriate.
parts.answer: Seeds in the same packet may not fail independently (e.g. a whole packet stored badly), or p may vary between packets
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The number of patients admitted to a small night clinic was recorded for 120 nights. No night had more than 5 admissions.
Admissions: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Nights: 15, 32, 35, 22, 10, 6
Show that the mean number of admissions per night is 1.983 to 4 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A Poisson model with this mean is fitted, with the final class taken as '5 or more'. Some of the expected frequencies are 16.51, 32.75, 21.47 and 10.65. Find the two missing expected frequencies (for 2 and for '5 or more').

parts.label: c
parts.text: Test at the 5% significance level whether a Poisson distribution fits the data.
parts.answer: X² = 0.407, ν = 4, critical value 9.488; 0.407 < 9.488, so do not reject H₀: a Poisson distribution fits the data
parts.working: B1 H₀: a Poisson distribution is a good model; H₁: it is not; M1 all six classes have E ≥ 5; M1 X² = Σ(O − E)²/E = 0.407; B1 ν = 4 (6 − 1 − 1, mean estimated), critical value 9.488; A1 0.407 < 9.488, so do not reject H₀: Poisson fits.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A transport survey in Lahore asked 200 commuters their usual mode of transport.
Under 30: bus 26, car 38, motorbike 16
30 and over: bus 54, car 32, motorbike 34
Test, at the 5% significance level, whether mode of transport is independent of age group.
parts.answer: X² = 9.16, ν = 2, critical value 5.991; 9.16 > 5.991, so reject H₀: mode of transport is associated with age group
parts.working: B1 H₀: mode of transport is independent of age group; H₁: they are not independent; M1 expected frequencies Eᵢⱼ = (row total × column total)/200: 32.00, 28.00, 20.00; 48.00, 42.00, 30.00; M1 X² = 9.16; B1 ν = 2, critical value 5.991; A1 9.16 > 5.991, so reject H₀: there is an association.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A tea company surveyed adults in three cities about their preferred hot drink.
Lahore: doodh patti 45, green tea 20, coffee 15
Karachi: doodh patti 38, green tea 30, coffee 22
Islamabad: doodh patti 27, green tea 30, coffee 23
Calculate the expected frequency for Islamabad and green tea under the hypothesis of independence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Test at the 5% significance level whether preferred drink is independent of city.
parts.answer: X² = 8.41, ν = 4, critical value 9.488; 8.41 < 9.488, so do not reject H₀: there is insufficient evidence that preferred drink depends on city
parts.working: B1 H₀: drink preference is independent of city; H₁: not independent; M1 expected frequencies Eᵢⱼ = (row total × column total)/250: 35.20, 25.60, 19.20; 39.60, 28.80, 21.60; 35.20, 25.60, 19.20; M1 X² = 8.41; B1 ν = 4, critical value 9.488; A1 8.41 < 9.488, so do not reject H₀: not associated.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Students at two hostels of a university in Jamshoro were asked what they usually eat for breakfast.
Hostel 1: paratha 34, cereal 20, nothing 16
Hostel 2: paratha 26, cereal 30, nothing 24
State the null and alternative hypotheses for a test of independence and find the number of degrees of freedom.
parts.answer: H₀: breakfast choice is independent of hostel; H₁: not independent; ν = (2 − 1)(3 − 1) = 2
parts.working: B1 hypotheses; B1 ν = 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Carry out the test at the 5% significance level.
parts.answer: X² = 4.02, ν = 2, critical value 5.991; 4.02 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: there is insufficient evidence that breakfast choice depends on hostel
parts.working: B1 hypotheses as in (a); M1 expected frequencies Eᵢⱼ = (row total × column total)/150: 28.00, 23.33, 18.67; 32.00, 26.67, 21.33; M1 X² = 4.02; B1 ν = 2, critical value 5.991; A1 4.02 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: not associated.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Students at a government school and a private school in Faisalabad were asked to name their favourite sport to play.
Government school: cricket 40, football 22, hockey 10, squash 3
Private school: cricket 30, football 33, hockey 8, squash 4
Calculate the expected frequencies for squash and explain why columns need to be combined.
parts.answer: 3.5 for each school; these are below 5, so squash is combined with hockey
parts.working: M1 75 × 7/150 = 3.5; A1 both 3.5; B1 expected frequencies less than 5 make the test unreliable, so merge squash and hockey.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Carry out the test at the 5% significance level to determine whether favourite sport is independent of type of school.
parts.answer: X² = 3.67, ν = 2, critical value 5.991; 3.67 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: there is insufficient evidence that favourite sport depends on type of school
parts.working: B1 H₀: favourite sport is independent of school type; H₁: not independent; M1 expected frequencies Eᵢⱼ = (row total × column total)/150: 35.00, 27.50, 12.50; 35.00, 27.50, 12.50 (columns cricket, football, hockey or squash); M1 X² = 3.67; B1 ν = 2, critical value 5.991; A1 3.67 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: not associated.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An agricultural researcher grows 180 wheat plants, 60 with each of three fertilisers A, B and C, and classifies each plant's growth as good or poor.

B: good 35, poor 25
C: good 23, poor 37
Test, at the 1% significance level, whether growth is independent of the fertiliser used.
parts.answer: X² = 12.5, ν = 2, critical value 9.210; 12.5 > 9.210, so reject H₀: growth depends on the fertiliser used
parts.working: B1 H₀: growth is independent of fertiliser; H₁: not independent; M1 expected frequencies Eᵢⱼ = (row total × column total)/180: 33.33, 26.67; 33.33, 26.67; 33.33, 26.67; M1 X² = 12.5; B1 ν = 2, critical value 9.210; A1 12.5 > 9.210, so reject H₀: growth depends on fertiliser.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: A: it has more good plants (42) than expected (33.33)
parts.working: B1

parts.text:
An education researcher records the grades of 220 A Level students according to how they mainly studied.
Self-study: grade A 18, grade B 30, grade C or below 32
Tuition centre: grade A 30, grade B 34, grade C or below 16
Online course: grade A 12, grade B 26, grade C or below 22
Test, at the 1% significance level, whether grade is independent of study method.
parts.answer: X² = 10.9, ν = 4, critical value 13.28; 10.9 < 13.28, so do not reject H₀: there is insufficient evidence of an association between grade and study method
parts.working: B1 H₀: grade is independent of study method; H₁: not independent; M1 expected frequencies Eᵢⱼ = (row total × column total)/220: 21.82, 32.73, 25.45; 21.82, 32.73, 25.45; 16.36, 24.55, 19.09; M1 X² = 10.9; B1 ν = 4, critical value 13.28; A1 10.9 < 13.28, so do not reject H₀: not associated.

parts.text:

Branch Q: satisfied 40, neutral 34, dissatisfied 26
Test, at the 10% significance level, whether satisfaction is independent of branch.
parts.answer: X² = 3.27, ν = 2, critical value 4.605; 3.27 < 4.605, so do not reject H₀: there is insufficient evidence that satisfaction depends on branch
parts.working: B1 H₀: satisfaction is independent of branch; H₁: not independent; M1 expected frequencies Eᵢⱼ = (row total × column total)/200: 46.00, 32.00, 22.00; 46.00, 32.00, 22.00; M1 X² = 3.27; B1 ν = 2, critical value 4.605; A1 3.27 < 4.605, so do not reject H₀: not associated.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A mobile network asked 180 customers in three age groups how satisfied they were with their service.
18–30: very satisfied 26, satisfied 16, unsatisfied 8, very unsatisfied 2
31–50: very satisfied 22, satisfied 30, unsatisfied 15, very unsatisfied 3
Over 50: very satisfied 12, satisfied 24, unsatisfied 18, very unsatisfied 4
Explain why the last two columns should be combined.
parts.answer: Expected frequencies for 'very unsatisfied' are 2.6, 3.5 and 2.9, all below 5
parts.working: M1 e.g. 52 × 9/180 = 2.6; A1 values below 5 so merge with 'unsatisfied'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Test at the 5% significance level whether satisfaction is independent of age group.
parts.answer: X² = 12.1, ν = 4, critical value 9.488; 12.1 > 9.488, so reject H₀: satisfaction is associated with age group
parts.working: B1 H₀: satisfaction is independent of age group; H₁: not independent; M1 expected frequencies Eᵢⱼ = (row total × column total)/180: 17.33, 20.22, 14.44; 23.33, 27.22, 19.44; 19.33, 22.56, 16.11; M1 X² = 12.1; B1 ν = 4, critical value 9.488; A1 12.1 > 9.488, so reject H₀: associated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the cell that contributes most to the test statistic and comment on it in context.
parts.answer: 18–30 and 'very satisfied', contribution 4.333: more customers aged 18–30 are very satisfied than expected under independence (26 observed against 17.33 expected)
parts.working: B1 correct cell with contribution; B1 comment comparing observed with expected.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A supermarket chain records the payment method used by 220 customers at a city-centre branch and at an out-of-town branch.
City centre: cash 34, card 46, mobile wallet 20 (total 100)
Out-of-town: cash 26, card 54, mobile wallet 40 (total 120)
Part of the table of expected frequencies is: city centre: cash 27.27, card —, mobile wallet 27.27; out-of-town: cash 32.73, card 54.55, mobile wallet —. Find the two missing expected frequencies.
parts.answer: city centre card 45.45; out-of-town mobile wallet 32.73
parts.working: M1 100 × 100/220 or by subtraction from row totals; A1 45.45 and 32.73.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The contributions (O − E)²/E for the city-centre cells are 1.659, 0.007 and 1.939. Calculate the remaining contributions and complete a test at the 5% significance level of whether payment method is independent of branch.
parts.answer: X² = 6.61, ν = 2, critical value 5.991; 6.61 > 5.991, so reject H₀: payment method depends on branch
parts.working: M1 out-of-town contributions 1.383, 0.005, 1.616; M1 X² = 6.61; B1 ν = 2, critical value 5.991; B1 H₀: payment method independent of branch, H₁: not independent; A1 6.61 > 5.991, so reject H₀: payment method depends on branch.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the payment habits at the two branches differ.
parts.answer: City-centre customers use cash more and mobile wallets less than expected; the reverse at the out-of-town branch
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A researcher in Hyderabad classifies 160 adults by whether they live in an urban or rural area and by their main source of news.

Rural: television 22, social media 35, newspaper 33

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the conclusion of the test at the 5% level and at the 1% level.
parts.answer: 5%: 7.26 > 5.991, so reject H₀: evidence of an association; 1%: 7.26 < 9.210, so do not reject H₀: no evidence of an association at this level
parts.working: B1 ν = 2; B1 5% critical value 5.991, conclusion; B1 1% critical value 9.210, conclusion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the different conclusions mean in terms of the probability of a Type I error.
parts.answer: The data are significant if we accept a 5% risk of wrongly rejecting a true H₀, but not if we require that risk to be only 1%
parts.working: B1

parts.text: A particle is projected from a point O on horizontal ground with speed u at an angle α above the horizontal. Show that its velocity is perpendicular to its initial velocity at time t = u/(g sin α).

parts.label: b

parts.text: A particle is projected from a point on horizontal ground with speed u at an angle α above the horizontal. Its greatest height is H and its range is R. Show that R = 4H cot α.
parts.working: M1 H = u² sin² α/(2g), R = 2u² sin α cos α/g; M1 R/H = 4 cos α/sin α; A1 (AG).
