parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prove by mathematical induction that, for all positive integers n,
Σ (from r = 1 to n) r(r + 2) = (1/6)n(n + 1)(2n + 7).
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: LHS = 1 × 3 = 3, RHS = (1/6)(1)(2)(9) = 3.
M1: assume true for n = k and add the (k + 1)th term (k + 1)(k + 3).
M1: factorise (1/6)(k + 1)[k(2k + 7) + 6(k + 3)] = (1/6)(k + 1)(2k² + 13k + 18).
A1: = (1/6)(k + 1)(k + 2)(2k + 9) = (1/6)(k + 1)((k + 1) + 1)(2(k + 1) + 7).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prove by mathematical induction that, for all positive integers n,
Σ (from r = 1 to n) 1/((2r − 1)(2r + 1)) = n/(2n + 1).
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: LHS = 1/(1 × 3) = 1/3, RHS = 1/3.
M1: assume true for n = k; add 1/((2k + 1)(2k + 3)).
M1: common denominator: [k(2k + 3) + 1]/((2k + 1)(2k + 3)) = (2k² + 3k + 1)/((2k + 1)(2k + 3)).
A1: = (k + 1)(2k + 1)/((2k + 1)(2k + 3)) = (k + 1)/(2(k + 1) + 1).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sequence u₁, u₂, u₃, … is defined by u₁ = 3 and u_(n+1) = 2u_n − 1 for n ≥ 1. Find u₅.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prove by mathematical induction that u_n = 2ⁿ + 1 for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 2¹ + 1 = 3 = u₁.
M1: assume u_k = 2ᵏ + 1; then u_(k+1) = 2(2ᵏ + 1) − 1.
A1: = 2^(k+1) + 1.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prove by mathematical induction that, for all positive integers n,
Σ (from r = 1 to n) r × r! = (n + 1)! − 1.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: LHS = 1 × 1! = 1, RHS = 2! − 1 = 1.
M1: assume true for n = k; add (k + 1)(k + 1)!.
M1: (k + 1)! − 1 + (k + 1)(k + 1)! = (k + 1)!(1 + k + 1) − 1.
A1: = (k + 2)(k + 1)! − 1 = (k + 2)! − 1.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prove by mathematical induction that, for all positive integers n,
Σ (from r = 1 to n) (2r − 1)² = (1/3)n(2n − 1)(2n + 1).
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: LHS = 1, RHS = (1/3)(1)(1)(3) = 1.
M1: assume true for n = k; add (2k + 1)².
M1: (1/3)(2k + 1)[k(2k − 1) + 3(2k + 1)] = (1/3)(2k + 1)(2k² + 5k + 3).
A1: = (1/3)(2k + 1)(k + 1)(2k + 3) = (1/3)(k + 1)(2(k + 1) − 1)(2(k + 1) + 1).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sequence u₁, u₂, u₃, … is defined by u₁ = 1 and u_(n+1) = 3u_n + 2. Prove by mathematical induction that u_n = 2 × 3^(n−1) − 1 for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 2 × 3⁰ − 1 = 1 = u₁.
M1: assume u_k = 2 × 3^(k−1) − 1; u_(k+1) = 3(2 × 3^(k−1) − 1) + 2.
A1: = 2 × 3ᵏ − 3 + 2 = 2 × 3ᵏ − 1.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the least value of n for which u_n > 10 000.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prove by mathematical induction that, for all positive integers n,
Σ (from r = 1 to n) r × 2ʳ = (n − 1)2^(n+1) + 2.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: LHS = 2, RHS = 0 + 2 = 2.
M1: assume true for n = k; add (k + 1)2^(k+1).
M1: (k − 1)2^(k+1) + (k + 1)2^(k+1) + 2 = 2k × 2^(k+1) + 2.
A1: = k × 2^(k+2) + 2 = ((k + 1) − 1)2^((k+1)+1) + 2.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the value of Σ (from r = 11 to 20) r × 2ʳ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove by mathematical induction that 2ⁿ > n² for all integers n ≥ 5.
parts.working:
B1: n = 5: 2⁵ = 32 > 25.
M1: assume 2ᵏ > k² for some k ≥ 5; then 2^(k+1) = 2 × 2ᵏ > 2k².
M1: 2k² − (k + 1)² = k² − 2k − 1 = (k − 1)² − 2 > 0 for k ≥ 5 (indeed for k ≥ 3).
A1: so 2^(k+1) > (k + 1)².
A1: true for n = 5 and true for k + 1 whenever true for k ≥ 5, so true for all n ≥ 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the values of n, with 1 ≤ n ≤ 4, for which 2ⁿ > n² is false.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sequence u₁, u₂, u₃, … is defined by u₁ = 2 and u_(n+1) = u_n/(1 + u_n). Prove by mathematical induction that u_n = 2/(2n − 1) for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 2/(2 − 1) = 2 = u₁.
M1: assume u_k = 2/(2k − 1); u_(k+1) = [2/(2k − 1)] ÷ [1 + 2/(2k − 1)].
M1: = [2/(2k − 1)] ÷ [(2k + 1)/(2k − 1)].
A1: = 2/(2k + 1) = 2/(2(k + 1) − 1).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of u₁₀₀ as a fraction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove by mathematical induction that 3ⁿ ≥ 2n² + 1 for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 3 ≥ 3 true.
M1: assume 3ᵏ ≥ 2k² + 1; then 3^(k+1) ≥ 3(2k² + 1) = 6k² + 3.
M1: compare with 2(k + 1)² + 1 = 2k² + 4k + 3.
M1: (6k² + 3) − (2k² + 4k + 3) = 4k² − 4k = 4k(k − 1) ≥ 0 for k ≥ 1.
A1: so 3^(k+1) ≥ 2(k + 1)² + 1.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sequence u₁, u₂, u₃, … is defined by u₁ = 1 and u_(n+1) = √(u_n + 6). Prove by mathematical induction that 0 < u_n < 3 for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 0 < 1 < 3.
M1: assume 0 < u_k < 3; then 6 < u_k + 6 < 9.
A1: so √6 < u_(k+1) < 3, hence 0 < u_(k+1) < 3.
A1: conclusion for all n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prove that u_(n+1) > u_n for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
M1: u_(n+1)² − u_n² = u_n + 6 − u_n² = −(u_n − 3)(u_n + 2).
A1: since 0 < u_n < 3, (u_n − 3) < 0 and (u_n + 2) > 0, so u_(n+1)² > u_n².
A1: both terms positive, so u_(n+1) > u_n.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find u₃ correct to 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sequence is defined by u₁ = 1, u₂ = 5 and u_(n+2) = 5u_(n+1) − 6u_n for n ≥ 1. Prove by mathematical induction that u_n = 3ⁿ − 2ⁿ for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 3 − 2 = 1; n = 2: 9 − 4 = 5 (both base cases needed).
M1: assume u_k = 3ᵏ − 2ᵏ and u_(k+1) = 3^(k+1) − 2^(k+1).
M1: u_(k+2) = 5(3^(k+1) − 2^(k+1)) − 6(3ᵏ − 2ᵏ).
M1: = 3ᵏ(15 − 6) − 2ᵏ(10 − 6) = 9 × 3ᵏ − 4 × 2ᵏ.
A1: = 3^(k+2) − 2^(k+2).
A1: true for n = 1, 2 and if true for n = k and k + 1 then true for k + 2, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find u₈.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Prove by mathematical induction that, for all positive integers n,
Σ (from r = 1 to n) 1/r² ≤ 2 − 1/n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 1 ≤ 2 − 1 = 1.
M1: assume Σ (1 to k) 1/r² ≤ 2 − 1/k; then Σ (1 to k + 1) ≤ 2 − 1/k + 1/(k + 1)².
M1: need −1/k + 1/(k + 1)² ≤ −1/(k + 1), i.e. 1/(k + 1)² ≤ 1/k − 1/(k + 1) = 1/(k(k + 1)).
A1: true since k(k + 1) < (k + 1)².
A1: so Σ (1 to k + 1) 1/r² ≤ 2 − 1/(k + 1).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce an upper bound for Σ (from r = 1 to ∞) 1/r².
parts.working: B1: 2 − 1/n < 2 for every n, so the partial sums are bounded above by 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A calculator algorithm for √3 uses u₁ = 2 and u_(n+1) = (u_n² + 3)/(2u_n). Find u₃ as an exact fraction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that u_(n+1) − √3 = (u_n − √3)²/(2u_n).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence prove by mathematical induction that u_n > √3 for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 2 > √3.
M1: assume u_k > √3 (so u_k > 0); by (b) u_(k+1) − √3 = (u_k − √3)²/(2u_k).
A1: numerator > 0 (as u_k ≠ √3) and denominator > 0, so u_(k+1) > √3.
A1: conclusion for all n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that y = x eˣ, prove by mathematical induction that dⁿy/dxⁿ = (x + n)eˣ for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: dy/dx = eˣ + x eˣ = (x + 1)eˣ.
M1: assume dᵏy/dxᵏ = (x + k)eˣ; differentiate using the product rule.
A1: d^(k+1)y/dx^(k+1) = eˣ + (x + k)eˣ = (x + k + 1)eˣ.
A1: form (x + (k + 1))eˣ clearly stated.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that f(x) = 1/(2x + 1), prove by mathematical induction that f⁽ⁿ⁾(x) = (−2)ⁿ n!/(2x + 1)^(n+1) for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: f′(x) = −2(2x + 1)⁻² = (−2)¹ 1!/(2x + 1)².
M1: assume f⁽ᵏ⁾(x) = (−2)ᵏ k!(2x + 1)^(−(k+1)); differentiate.
A1: f⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾(x) = (−2)ᵏ k! × (−(k + 1)) × 2 × (2x + 1)^(−(k+2)).
A1: = (−2)^(k+1)(k + 1)!/(2x + 1)^(k+2).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the value of f⁽⁴⁾(0).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that y = ln(1 + x), x > −1, prove by mathematical induction that dⁿy/dxⁿ = (−1)^(n−1)(n − 1)!/(1 + x)ⁿ for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: dy/dx = 1/(1 + x) = (−1)⁰ 0!/(1 + x)¹.
M1: assume dᵏy/dxᵏ = (−1)^(k−1)(k − 1)!(1 + x)^(−k); differentiate.
A1: = (−1)^(k−1)(k − 1)! × (−k)(1 + x)^(−k−1).
A1: = (−1)ᵏ k!/(1 + x)^(k+1).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence write down the coefficient of x⁶ in the Maclaurin series for ln(1 + x).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that y = sin 3x, prove by mathematical induction that dⁿy/dxⁿ = 3ⁿ sin(3x + nπ/2) for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: dy/dx = 3 cos 3x = 3 sin(3x + π/2).
M1: assume dᵏy/dxᵏ = 3ᵏ sin(3x + kπ/2); differentiate.
A1: d^(k+1)y/dx^(k+1) = 3^(k+1) cos(3x + kπ/2).
A1: = 3^(k+1) sin(3x + kπ/2 + π/2) = 3^(k+1) sin(3x + (k + 1)π/2).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of d⁵y/dx⁵ when x = π/9.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Given that y = x² e^(2x), prove by mathematical induction that
dⁿy/dxⁿ = 2^(n−2) e^(2x) (4x² + 4nx + n(n − 1)) for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: dy/dx = 2x e^(2x) + 2x² e^(2x) = 2⁻¹ e^(2x)(4x² + 4x) ✓.
M1: assume true for n = k; differentiate the product.
M1: d/dx[2^(k−2) e^(2x)(4x² + 4kx + k(k − 1))] = 2^(k−2) e^(2x)[2(4x² + 4kx + k² − k) + 8x + 4k].
A1: = 2^(k−1) e^(2x)[4x² + 4(k + 1)x + k² + k].
A1: k² + k = (k + 1)k, giving the formula with n = k + 1.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that y = eˣ cos x, prove by mathematical induction that dⁿy/dxⁿ = 2^(n/2) eˣ cos(x + nπ/4) for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: dy/dx = eˣ(cos x − sin x) = √2 eˣ cos(x + π/4).
M1: assume dᵏy/dxᵏ = 2^(k/2) eˣ cos(x + kπ/4); differentiate.
A1: = 2^(k/2) eˣ[cos(x + kπ/4) − sin(x + kπ/4)].
M1: use cos A − sin A = √2 cos(A + π/4).
A1: = 2^((k+1)/2) eˣ cos(x + (k + 1)π/4).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the value of d⁸y/dx⁸ when x = 0.
parts.working: B1: 2⁴ × e⁰ × cos 2π = 16.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Given that y = x ln x, x > 0, prove by mathematical induction that, for all integers n ≥ 2,
dⁿy/dxⁿ = (−1)ⁿ (n − 2)!/x^(n−1).
parts.working:
M1: dy/dx = ln x + 1.
B1: n = 2: d²y/dx² = 1/x = (−1)² 0!/x¹.
M1: assume dᵏy/dxᵏ = (−1)ᵏ (k − 2)! x^(−(k−1)); differentiate.
A1: = (−1)ᵏ (k − 2)! × (−(k − 1)) x^(−k).
A1: = (−1)^(k+1) (k − 1)!/xᵏ, the formula with n = k + 1.
A1: true for n = 2 and true for k + 1 when true for k ≥ 2, so true for all n ≥ 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of d⁶y/dx⁶ when x = 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove by mathematical induction that 5ⁿ + 3 is divisible by 4 for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 5 + 3 = 8 = 4 × 2.
M1: assume 5ᵏ + 3 = 4m for some integer m.
M1: 5^(k+1) + 3 = 5 × 5ᵏ + 3 = 5(4m − 3) + 3.
A1: = 20m − 12 = 4(5m − 3), divisible by 4.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove by mathematical induction that 7ⁿ − 3ⁿ is divisible by 4 for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 7 − 3 = 4.
M1: assume 7ᵏ − 3ᵏ = 4m.
M1: 7^(k+1) − 3^(k+1) = 7 × 7ᵏ − 3 × 3ᵏ = 7(7ᵏ − 3ᵏ) + 4 × 3ᵏ.
A1: = 28m + 4 × 3ᵏ = 4(7m + 3ᵏ), divisible by 4.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let f(n) = n³ + 5n. Show that f(n + 1) − f(n) = 3n(n + 1) + 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence prove by mathematical induction that n³ + 5n is divisible by 6 for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: f(1) = 6.
M1: assume 6 | f(k); f(k + 1) = f(k) + 3k(k + 1) + 6.
A1: k(k + 1) is a product of consecutive integers, so even; hence 3k(k + 1) is divisible by 6, and so f(k + 1) is divisible by 6.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove by mathematical induction that 3^(2n) + 7 is divisible by 8 for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 9 + 7 = 16 = 8 × 2.
M1: assume 3^(2k) + 7 = 8m.
M1: 3^(2k+2) + 7 = 9 × 3^(2k) + 7 = 9(8m − 7) + 7.
A1: = 72m − 56 = 8(9m − 7).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the remainder when 3^(2n) + 7 is divided by 16 in the case n = 2. Hence explain why the statement '3^(2n) + 7 is divisible by 16 for all positive integers n' is false, even though it is true for n = 1.
parts.answer: Remainder 8; n = 2 is a counter-example (88 is not a multiple of 16).
parts.working:
M1: n = 2: 81 + 7 = 88 = 5 × 16 + 8.
A1: remainder 8 ≠ 0, so one counter-example disproves the statement; a true base case alone proves nothing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove by mathematical induction that 2^(n+2) + 3^(2n+1) is divisible by 7 for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 2³ + 3³ = 8 + 27 = 35 = 7 × 5.
M1: assume 2^(k+2) + 3^(2k+1) = 7m.
M1: 2^(k+3) + 3^(2k+3) = 2 × 2^(k+2) + 9 × 3^(2k+1).
M1: = 2(2^(k+2) + 3^(2k+1)) + 7 × 3^(2k+1).
A1: = 14m + 7 × 3^(2k+1) = 7(2m + 3^(2k+1)).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove by mathematical induction that 4^(n+1) + 5^(2n−1) is divisible by 21 for all positive integers n.
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: 4² + 5¹ = 21.
M1: assume 4^(k+1) + 5^(2k−1) = 21m.
M1: 4^(k+2) + 5^(2k+1) = 4 × 4^(k+1) + 25 × 5^(2k−1).
M1: = 4(4^(k+1) + 5^(2k−1)) + 21 × 5^(2k−1).
A1: = 21(4m + 5^(2k−1)), divisible by 21.
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The matrix A is given by A = (2 1; 0 1), where rows are separated by a semicolon. Prove by mathematical induction that, for all positive integers n,
Aⁿ = (2ⁿ  2ⁿ − 1; 0  1).
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: (2 1; 0 1) = A.
M1: assume Aᵏ = (2ᵏ 2ᵏ − 1; 0 1); form A^(k+1) = Aᵏ A.
A1: = (2^(k+1)  2ᵏ + 2ᵏ − 1; 0  1).
A1: = (2^(k+1)  2^(k+1) − 1; 0 1).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence write down A¹⁰.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The matrix M is given by M = (4 −3; 2 −1), rows separated by a semicolon. Prove by mathematical induction that, for all positive integers n,
Mⁿ = (3 × 2ⁿ − 2   3 − 3 × 2ⁿ ; 2^(n+1) − 2   3 − 2^(n+1)).
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: (6 − 2, 3 − 6; 4 − 2, 3 − 4) = (4 −3; 2 −1) = M.
M1: assume formula for Mᵏ; form M^(k+1) = Mᵏ M.
M1: top-left: 4(3 × 2ᵏ − 2) + 2(3 − 3 × 2ᵏ) = 6 × 2ᵏ − 2 = 3 × 2^(k+1) − 2; top-right: −3(3 × 2ᵏ − 2) − (3 − 3 × 2ᵏ) = 3 − 6 × 2ᵏ = 3 − 3 × 2^(k+1).
A1: bottom-left: 4(2^(k+1) − 2) + 2(3 − 2^(k+1)) = 2^(k+2) − 2.
A1: bottom-right: −3(2^(k+1) − 2) − (3 − 2^(k+1)) = 3 − 2^(k+2).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find M⁵.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The 3 × 3 matrix B has rows (1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1) and (0, 0, 1). Prove by mathematical induction that, for all positive integers n, Bⁿ has rows
(1, n, n(n − 1)/2), (0, 1, n) and (0, 0, 1).
parts.working:
B1: n = 1: rows (1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1), (0, 0, 1) = B.
M1: assume formula for Bᵏ; form B^(k+1) = Bᵏ B.
A1: first row: (1, 1 + k, k + k(k − 1)/2).
M1: k + k(k − 1)/2 = k(k + 1)/2 = (k + 1)((k + 1) − 1)/2.
A1: second row (0, 1, 1 + k), third row (0, 0, 1).
A1: correct conclusion stating that the result is true for n = k + 1 when true for n = k, and true for n = 1, so true for all positive integers n.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 0.2 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 0.5 m. The other end is attached to a fixed point O. The particle is released from rest at O and its lowest point is 1.3 m below O. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the modulus of elasticity of the string.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest speed of the particle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the acceleration of the particle at its lowest point.
parts.working:
M1: tension = λ(0.8)/0.5 = 6.5 N; 6.5 − 2 = 0.2a
A1: a = 22.5 m s⁻² upwards

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 0.5 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 1 m and modulus of elasticity 10 N. The other end of the string is fixed at a point O on a rough horizontal surface; the coefficient of friction is 0.2. The particle is released from rest with the string stretched along the surface to a length of 1.6 m. The particle can pass over O without obstruction. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the speed of the particle when the string becomes slack.
parts.working:
B1: friction = 0.2 × 5 = 1 N (and tension 6 N > 1 N, so it moves)
M1: EPE = 10(0.6²)/2 = 1.8 J; work against friction = 1 × 0.6
M1: ½(0.5)v² = 1.8 − 0.6
A1: v² = 4.8, v = 2.19 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the total distance travelled by the particle before it comes to rest, and state where it comes to rest.
parts.answer: 1.8 m; 0.2 m beyond O (on the opposite side from its starting point)
parts.working:
M1: slack string: deceleration 1/0.5 = 2 m s⁻²
M1: distance = 4.8/(2 × 2) = 1.2 m
B1: 1.2 m < 2 m, so the string does not become taut again on the other side
A1: total 0.6 + 1.2 = 1.8 m; stops 0.2 m past O

parts.label: a
parts.text:
When a particle of mass 0.3 kg hangs in equilibrium from a light spring, the length of the spring is 0.65 m. When the particle is replaced by one of mass 0.5 kg, the length in equilibrium is 0.75 m. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the natural length and the modulus of elasticity of the spring.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two fixed points A and B are 2 m apart, with A vertically above B. A particle P of mass 0.5 kg is attached to A by a light spring of natural length 0.8 m and modulus of elasticity 20 N, and to B by a light spring of natural length 0.8 m and modulus of elasticity 30 N. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the length AP when P is in equilibrium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the lower spring is stretched or compressed in this position.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 1.2 kg is attached to one end of each of two identical light elastic strings, each of natural length 0.6 m. The other ends of the strings are attached to the points A and B, which are 1.6 m apart on the same horizontal level. In equilibrium the particle is 0.6 m vertically below the mid-point of AB. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the tension in each string.
parts.working:
B1: each string has length √(0.8² + 0.6²) = 1 m; cos θ = 0.6 with the vertical
M1: 2T(0.6) = 12
A1: T = 10 N

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the modulus of elasticity of the strings.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 2 kg rests on a smooth plane inclined at an angle θ to the horizontal, where sin θ = 0.6. It is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 0.8 m and modulus of elasticity 40 N; the other end is fixed to a point higher up the same line of greatest slope. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the extension of the string in equilibrium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A horizontal force of magnitude P N, acting in the vertical plane containing the line of greatest slope and towards the plane, is now applied so that the particle rests in equilibrium with the string at its natural length. Find P.
parts.working:
M1: resolve along slope: P cos θ = 20 sin θ
A1: P × 0.8 = 12
A1: P = 15

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 4 kg is on a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal, where the coefficient of friction is 0.2. It is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 1 m and modulus of elasticity 50 N; the other end of the string is fixed at a point O higher up the same line of greatest slope. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the least and greatest possible distances of the particle from O when it is in equilibrium. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.working:
B1: R = 40 cos 30° = 34.64 N, F_max = 0.2R = 6.928 N
M1: least extension when friction acts up the slope: T + F = 40 sin 30°
A1: T = 13.07 N, x = T/50 = 0.261 m, distance 1.26 m
M1: greatest when friction acts down the slope: T = 20 + F
A1: T = 26.93 N, x = 0.539 m
A1: distance 1.54 m

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A uniform rod AB of mass 3 kg and length 1.2 m is freely hinged at A to a vertical wall. It is held horizontally in equilibrium by a light elastic string of natural length 1.2 m joining B to the point C on the wall 0.9 m vertically above A. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find the tension in the string.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the modulus of elasticity of the string.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the magnitude of the force exerted by the hinge on the rod.
parts.working:
M1: horizontal: H = 25 × 0.8 = 20 N
M1: vertical: V = 30 − 25 × 0.6 = 15 N
A1: √(20² + 15²) = 25 N

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A particle of mass 0.6 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 0.5 m and modulus of elasticity 12 N. The other end of the string is fixed at O. The particle is held in equilibrium by a horizontal force of magnitude P N, with the string inclined at angle θ to the downward vertical, where tan θ = 3/4. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
Find P and the tension in the string.
parts.working:
M1: resolve vertically: T cos θ = 6, T = 6/0.8
A1: T = 7.5 N
A1: P = T sin θ = 4.5

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the depth of the particle below O.
parts.working:
M1: extension = 7.5 × 0.5/12 = 0.3125 m
M1: length 0.8125 m; depth = 0.8125 cos θ
A1: 0.65 m

parts.label: c
parts.text: The force is changed so that, in a new equilibrium, the string is inclined at 60° to the downward vertical, with the horizontal force still acting. Find the new length of the string.
parts.working:
M1: T cos 60° = 6, T = 12 N
A1: extension = 12 × 0.5/12 = 0.5 m, length 1 m

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the definitions of sinh x and cosh x in terms of exponentials, prove that cosh²x − sinh²x = 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that sinh x = 3/4, find the exact value of cosh x and of tanh x.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the exact values of sinh(ln 4) and tanh(ln 4), giving each as a fraction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the definitions sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2 and cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2. Prove that sinh 2x = 2 sinh x cosh x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that cosh x = 13/12 and x > 0, find the exact value of sinh 2x.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the definitions sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2 and cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2. Prove that cosh 2x = 2cosh²x − 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that cosh x = 3, find the value of cosh 2x and of cosh 4x.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express 4 cosh x − 2 sinh x in terms of eˣ, simplifying your answer.
parts.working:
M1: 2(eˣ + e⁻ˣ) − (eˣ − e⁻ˣ).
A1: = eˣ + 3e⁻ˣ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the minimum value of 4 cosh x − 2 sinh x and the exact value of x at which it occurs.
parts.working:
M1: differentiate: eˣ − 3e⁻ˣ = 0 ⇒ e^(2x) = 3.
A1: x = (1/2) ln 3 (second derivative eˣ + 3e⁻ˣ > 0, so a minimum).
A1: value √3 + 3/√3 = 2√3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Starting from cosh²x − sinh²x = 1, prove that coth²x − 1 = cosech²x for x ≠ 0.
parts.working:
M1: divide every term by sinh²x (sinh x ≠ 0 for x ≠ 0).
A1: cosh²x/sinh²x − 1 = 1/sinh²x, i.e. coth²x − 1 = cosech²x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that coth x = −5/3, find the exact value of cosech x.
parts.working:
M1: cosech²x = 25/9 − 1 = 16/9.
A1: coth x < 0 ⇒ x < 0 ⇒ sinh x < 0, so cosech x = −4/3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that (cosh x + sinh x)ⁿ = cosh nx + sinh nx for any positive integer n.
parts.working:
M1: cosh x + sinh x = eˣ, so (cosh x + sinh x)ⁿ = e^(nx).
A1: e^(nx) = cosh nx + sinh nx.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence, or otherwise, find the exact value of (cosh(ln 2) + sinh(ln 2))⁵ − (cosh(ln 2) − sinh(ln 2))⁵.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove that arsinh x = ln(x + √(x² + 1)).
parts.working:
M1: let y = arsinh x, so x = sinh y = (e^y − e^(−y))/2.
M1: e^(2y) − 2x e^y − 1 = 0, a quadratic in e^y.
A1: e^y = x ± √(x² + 1).
A1: e^y > 0 rejects the minus sign, so y = ln(x + √(x² + 1)).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of arsinh(3/4) − arsinh(−4/3).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove that arcosh x = ln(x + √(x² − 1)) for x ≥ 1.
parts.working:
M1: y = arcosh x (y ≥ 0), x = (e^y + e^(−y))/2.
M1: e^(2y) − 2x e^y + 1 = 0.
A1: e^y = x ± √(x² − 1).
A1: y ≥ 0 needs e^y ≥ 1; the product of the roots is 1, so the larger root x + √(x² − 1) is taken.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of arcosh(5/3) + arcosh(17/8), simplifying your answer to a single logarithm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove that artanh x = (1/2) ln((1 + x)/(1 − x)) for −1 < x < 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express artanh(1/3) + artanh(1/5) as a single logarithm.

parts.text: Using exponentials, prove that sinh 3x = 3 sinh x + 4 sinh³x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that sinh x = 1/2, find the exact value of sinh 3x.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the definitions sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2 and cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2. Prove that cosh(x + y) = cosh x cosh y + sinh x sinh y.
parts.working:
M1: cosh x cosh y = (e^(x+y) + e^(x−y) + e^(−x+y) + e^(−x−y))/4.
M1: sinh x sinh y = (e^(x+y) − e^(x−y) − e^(−x+y) + e^(−x−y))/4.
M1: add: (2e^(x+y) + 2e^(−x−y))/4.
A1: = cosh(x + y).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that sinh a = 3/4 and sinh b = 5/12, with a, b > 0, find the exact value of cosh(a + b).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove that 1 − tanh²x = sech²x.
parts.working:
M1: divide cosh²x − sinh²x = 1 by cosh²x.
A1: 1 − tanh²x = sech²x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that tanh x = −5/13, find the exact values of cosh x and sinh x.
parts.working:
M1: sech²x = 1 − 25/169 = 144/169.
A1: cosh x = 13/12 (cosh x ≥ 1).
A1: sinh x = tanh x cosh x = −5/12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that x = ln(2 + √3), find the exact values of cosh x, sinh x and tanh x.
parts.answer: cosh x = 2, sinh x = √3, tanh x = √3/2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that cosh 2t = (1 + tanh²t)/(1 − tanh²t).
parts.working:
M1: cosh 2t = cosh²t + sinh²t.
M1: divide numerator and denominator by cosh²t, using cosh²t − sinh²t = 1.
A1: = (1 + tanh²t)/(1 − tanh²t).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of cosh(2 artanh(1/2)).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using exponentials, prove that cosh 3x = 4cosh³x − 3 cosh x.
parts.working:
M1: 4cosh³x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)³/2 = (e^(3x) + 3eˣ + 3e⁻ˣ + e^(−3x))/2.
M1: 3 cosh x = (3eˣ + 3e⁻ˣ)/2.
M1: subtract.
A1: = (e^(3x) + e^(−3x))/2 = cosh 3x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that cosh x = 5/4, find the exact value of cosh 3x, and verify your answer by first finding x as a logarithm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the result for tanh(x + y) in terms of tanh x and tanh y, which you should first prove from the addition formulae for sinh and cosh, show that tanh 2x = 2 tanh x/(1 + tanh²x).
parts.working:
M1: tanh(x + y) = (sinh x cosh y + cosh x sinh y)/(cosh x cosh y + sinh x sinh y).
M1: divide top and bottom by cosh x cosh y.
A1: = (tanh x + tanh y)/(1 + tanh x tanh y).
A1: put y = x: tanh 2x = 2 tanh x/(1 + tanh²x).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that tanh 2x = 4/5, find the exact value of tanh x.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express 5 cosh x + 3 sinh x in the form R cosh(x + α), where R > 0, giving R exactly and α as a logarithm.
parts.working:
M1: R cosh x cosh α + R sinh x sinh α: R cosh α = 5, R sinh α = 3.
A1: R² = 25 − 9 = 16, R = 4.
M1: tanh α = 3/5 ⇒ α = (1/2) ln((1 + 3/5)/(1 − 3/5)).
A1: α = (1/2) ln 4 = ln 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the minimum value of 5 cosh x + 3 sinh x and the value of x at which it occurs.
parts.working:
B1: minimum of cosh is 1 when x + ln 2 = 0.
B1: value 4 at x = −ln 2.

parts.text: Prove that sinh x + sinh y = 2 sinh((x + y)/2) cosh((x − y)/2).

parts.text: Hence show that sinh 3x + sinh x = 0 has only one real solution.
parts.working:

parts.label: a
parts.text: By writing each side in logarithmic form, show that artanh x = arsinh(x/√(1 − x²)) for −1 < x < 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use this result to find the exact value of x for which artanh x = arsinh(1).
parts.working:
M1: x/√(1 − x²) = 1 ⇒ x² = 1 − x².
A1: x = 1/√2 (positive since arsinh 1 > 0).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that cosh 2y = 2cosh²y − 1 and hence prove that arcosh(2x² − 1) = 2 arcosh x for x ≥ 1.
parts.working:
B1: cosh 2y = 2cosh²y − 1 (from exponentials or cosh 2y = cosh²y + sinh²y).
M1: let y = arcosh x ≥ 0, so cosh y = x.
M1: cosh 2y = 2x² − 1, and 2y ≥ 0.
A1: so 2y = arcosh(2x² − 1), i.e. arcosh(2x² − 1) = 2 arcosh x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of arcosh 7 in terms of a single logarithm of a number of the form a + b√3, where a and b are integers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that sinh x = −2, find the exact values of cosh x and tanh x.
parts.working:
M1: cosh²x = 1 + 4 = 5, cosh x > 0.
A1: cosh x = √5, tanh x = −2/√5 = −2√5/5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact value of x, and show that sinh 2x + cosh 2x = 9 − 4√5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation cosh 2x − 5 sinh x = 4, giving your answers as logarithms in exact form.
parts.working:
M1: use cosh 2x = 1 + 2sinh²x.
M1: 2sinh²x − 5 sinh x − 3 = 0.
A1: (2 sinh x + 1)(sinh x − 3) = 0, sinh x = 3 or −1/2.
A1: x = ln(3 + √10).
A1: x = ln(−1/2 + √(5/4)) = ln((√5 − 1)/2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation 2 cosh 2x − 9 cosh x + 7 = 0, giving your answers in exact logarithmic form where appropriate.
parts.working:
M1: cosh 2x = 2cosh²x − 1.
M1: 4cosh²x − 9 cosh x + 5 = 0.
A1: (cosh x − 1)(4 cosh x − 5) = 0.
A1: cosh x = 1 ⇒ x = 0.
A1: cosh x = 5/4 ⇒ x = ±ln 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation 3 sech²x + 4 tanh x + 1 = 0, giving your answer in the form a ln b.
parts.working:
M1: sech²x = 1 − tanh²x.
M1: 3tanh²x − 4 tanh x − 4 = 0.
A1: (3 tanh x + 2)(tanh x − 2) = 0.
A1: tanh x = 2 rejected (|tanh x| < 1); tanh x = −2/3.
A1: x = (1/2) ln((1/3)/(5/3)) = −(1/2) ln 5.

parts.label: a

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that sinh 3x = 3 sinh x + 4 sinh³x, solve the equation sinh 3x = 7 sinh x, giving the non-zero solutions as logarithms in exact form.
parts.working:
M1: 4sinh³x − 4 sinh x = 0.
M1: 4 sinh x (sinh x − 1)(sinh x + 1) = 0.
A1: sinh x = 0 ⇒ x = 0.
A1: sinh x = 1 ⇒ x = ln(1 + √2).
A1: sinh x = −1 ⇒ x = ln(√2 − 1) = −ln(1 + √2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the equation tanh x + sech x = 7/5 can be written as e^(2x) − 5eˣ + 6 = 0.
parts.working:
M1: multiply by cosh x: sinh x + 1 = (7/5) cosh x.
M1: (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2 + 1 = (7/10)(eˣ + e⁻ˣ); multiply by 10eˣ.
M1: 5e^(2x) − 5 + 10eˣ = 7e^(2x) + 7.
A1: 2e^(2x) − 10eˣ + 12 = 0 ⇒ e^(2x) − 5eˣ + 6 = 0.
